concept: Solana wallet and transaction building for bots
summary: Source-anchored leads on building, signing and landing Solana transactions from a bot: keypair handling (solders, solana-py, @solana/web3.js, @solana/kit), legacy/v0/v1 transactions and address lookup tables, blockhash expiry and commitment, compute budget and priority fees, simulateTransaction and preflight, and Jito bundles. Drawn from 568 research units over 223 cited sources (github.com, docs.jito.wtf, helius.dev, anza.xyz and others). Evidence status: research claims ungated (v4 evidence gate not passed); treat as leads with cited sources.

facts.text: @solana/kit is the renamed 2.x line of @solana/web3.js. It is functional (no classes except SolanaError), fully tree-shakable, uses Web Crypto Ed25519 so key and signing operations are async, supports native bigint, and has zero third-party dependencies. It is not backward-compatible with web3.js 1.x.

@solana/kit is the renamed 2.x line of @solana/web3.js (the npm package @solana/kit was created 2025-02-27). It is functional (no classes except SolanaError), tree-shakable, has no third-party dependencies, signs with native Ed25519 through Web Crypto, and returns 64-bit RPC values as bigint. It is a complete breaking change from web3.js 1.x, so a migration means rewriting call sites; the @solana/compat package converts between legacy and Kit types.

@solana/kit is the renamed 2.x line of @solana/web3.js, not an incremental release: its README calls it 'a complete and total breaking change' from 1.x. Kit is function-based (no classes except SolanaError), fully tree-shakable, uses the runtime's native Web Crypto Ed25519 (key generation, import, signing and verification are async; a polyfill covers runtimes without it) and native bigint. Its npm manifest (8.6.0) lists 27 direct dependencies, all @solana/* packages, matching the README's claim of no third-party dependencies.

Kit has no Connection or Transaction classes. Moving a web3.js v1 codebase to Kit means rewriting every call site, and libraries such as Anchor's TypeScript client did not plug into Kit. The @solana/compat package offers conversion helpers between legacy and Kit types.

FullSend is a separate, access-form-gated Jito service: a Solana-compatible JSON-RPC sendTransaction at https://mainnet.hudson.jito.wtf with an api_key query parameter, direct-to-leader SWQOS delivery, validator blacklists for MEV protection (default and custom, both on by default), and a browser-safe sendTransactionWeb that authenticates by authorized fee-payer signer. It runs no simulation and tracks no confirmation. Jito's BAM changelog says FullSend users needed no action during the Alpenglow BAM maintenance window.

Do not catch -32015 and return null or 'not found'. It means the request failed on a versioned transaction, not that the transaction is missing. Helius says -32015 in logs already shows a project failing on versioned transactions. A payment-detection loop that swallows it reports a landed transaction as lost.

solana-keychain is a Solana Foundation signer library with Rust, TypeScript (Solana Kit compatible), Python (on solders) and Go implementations behind one interface. Its README lists Memory, Vault, Privy, Turnkey, AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Fireblocks, Dfns, Para, CDP, Crossmint, Openfort, Utila and Fordefi backends, plus an opt-in, Rust-only Ledger backend marked unaudited. The README says OtterSec audited the four implementations (Ledger out of scope) after an earlier Accretion audit. docs.rs lists Rust crate 2.0.0 released 1 October 2026, owned by solana-foundation-tech; Kora builds its signers on i
The base fee is a flat 5,000 lamports per required signature. It does not depend on the CUs the transaction requests or uses. The priority fee is charged on top of the base fee.

A v0 message is a legacy message plus a 0x80 version prefix byte and an address_table_lookups array after the instructions. Each lookup names a table by its 32-byte address and lists one-byte writable and read-only indexes into it. The runtime appends the resolved writable addresses, then the read-only ones, to the static keys, and instructions index into that combined list. A lookup that selects no accounts fails sanitization.

New table entries are not usable in the slot where they were added. The table stores last_extended_slot and last_extended_slot_start_index. While the current slot equals last_extended_slot, a lookup sees only the entries before that start index. A transaction that references a newer entry in the same slot fails.

A null entry from getSignatureStatuses means the status was not found, not that the transaction failed. The method searches only a recent status cache unless searchTransactionHistory is true. A null can mean dropped, never landed, or evicted from the cache. Treat the transaction as dead only after block height passes lastValidBlockHeight and a history search also returns null.

A keypair file written by solana-keygen is a JSON array of exactly 64 byte values: the first 32 bytes are the Ed25519 secret seed and the last 32 bytes are the public key. Metaplex states the file 'must be a JSON array of 64 numbers'.

A 32-byte value is a seed, not a secret key, and the constructors treat it differently. Rust keypair_from_seed fails with 'Seed is too short' under 32 bytes and silently ignores bytes past 32 (inferred from code). web3.js Keypair.fromSeed has no length check in its own code and builds the 64-byte secretKey as seed followed by derived pubkey. Passing a 32-byte seed to the 64-byte-only loaders fails, and passing 64 bytes to a seed constructor is a likely mix-up.

A Solana CLI keypair file is a JSON array of exactly 64 byte values: the first 32 are the Ed25519 secret seed and the last 32 are the public key. `solana-keygen new` writes it to ~/.config/solana/id.json unless --outfile is given (Agave builds home_dir/.config/solana/id.json). Metaplex states the file 'must be a JSON array of 64 numbers'.

getSignatureStatuses takes up to 256 signatures. A null entry means no status was found (never landed, dropped, or evicted), not that the transaction failed. Without searchTransactionHistory it searches only the recent status cache, which holds active slots plus MAX_RECENT_BLOCKHASHES (300) rooted slots. A confirmations value of null means rooted and finalized. Check err on every non-null entry.

A passing simulation is a snapshot, not a guarantee. It runs against the bank state at simulation time, and execution later checks the live state. Jupiter lists `SlippageToleranceExceeded` (6001) and DEX tick-array errors, where the market 'moved out of range', as swap failures, and Triton notes that `processed` state can change if the cluster switches forks.

Commitment names: processed is the node's newest view of its best fork and can change if the cluster switches forks; confirmed is the highest slot that at least two thirds of active stake voted on; finalized is the highest slot the cluster recognises as final. The Solana Alpenglow page says all three 'still mean what they meant before'.

getLatestBlockhash returns lastValidBlockHeight = block_height + 150 - age for the bank chosen by the request commitment (Agave get_blockhash_last_valid_block_height). A mainnet check on 2026-11-06 returned a lastValidBlockHeight 149 or 150 blocks above the same-commitment getBlockHeight, as expected for a fresh blockhash. lastValidBlockHeight is not part of the signed transaction, so the sender must store it beside the transaction.

Jito's checklist for a bundle that is not landing: validate the transactions with simulateTransaction and the bundle with simulateBundle on Jito-Solana RPC; look the bundle ID up in the Jito explorer or call getInflightBundleStatuses within 5 minutes; compare the tip with current tip-floor percentiles; and count the latency to every component you touch.

Bots commonly receive the key as a string in an env var in either of two shapes: the JSON byte array from solana-keygen or a base58 string. Solders exposes both constructors (from_bytes for 64 raw bytes, from_base58_string). One Rust trading SDK (sol-trade-sdk 5.0.0) trims the input, treats a leading '[' as a JSON byte array, otherwise base58-decodes, then enforces len == 64 ('keypair must contain 64 bytes, got N') and rejects placeholder text and short arrays.

A base58 Solana secret key is the base58 encoding of the full 64-byte keypair (32-byte seed plus 32-byte public key), not of the 32-byte seed. `Keypair::try_from_base58_string` in solana-keypair decodes into a 64-byte buffer. kora-lib fails any other length with 'Invalid private key length: expected 64 bytes, got N', and sol-trade-sdk fails with 'keypair must contain 64 bytes, got N'. `Keypair::from_base58_string` panics on malformed input, and sol-trade-sdk wrote its own loader to avoid that panic.

A Solana keypair file is plaintext and the generation passphrase does not protect it. Anza's file-system wallet page says 'This file contains your unencrypted keypair', 'File system wallets are the least secure method of storing SOL tokens', and that even with a password 'that password applies to the recovery seed phrase, not the file'. Matt Mazur's walkthrough shows the CLI prompt itself saying the passphrase improves the seed phrase 'NOT the keypair file itself, which is stored as insecure plain text'. Anza's page gives no file-permission advice.

In Rust, write_keypair_file calls EncodableKey::write_to_file (solana-signer 4.0.0): it creates missing parent directories, opens with create + truncate, and on Unix sets mode 0o600; on non-Unix targets no mode is set. solana-keypair has a Unix-only test asserting 0o600. `solana-keygen new` writes through output_keypair -> write_keypair_file, and Agave's keygen.rs contains no mode code of its own, so CLI-created key files get 0600 on Unix at creation. The wall-clock length of the 150-block window has roughly halved. SIMD-0525 (Anza, status Activated) cut the target slot time from 400 ms to 200 ms in four feature-gated steps (350, 300, 250, 200 ms) and left the blockhash-queue size unchanged, so anything counted in slots now takes less time. On 2026-11-06 all four feature gates were active on mainnet (the 200 ms gate activated at slot 454,464,000, epoch 1052, on 2026-10-08) and recent performance samples showed 212 to 217 ms per slot. 150 blocks therefore last about 32 s, plus time for skipped slots. In Python, solders (Rust-backed bindings by Kevin Heavey) supplies the core types: Keypair, Pubkey, Instruction, MessageV0, VersionedTransaction, signing and serialization, RPC request and response types, and an in-process LiteSVM. solders does not fetch blockhashes or send transactions; solana-py's AsyncClient does (get_latest_blockhash, send_transaction). solana-py builds on solders types, and its README says anything missing from it 'is probably in solders now'. Solana's docs name both packages and recommend solana-py for networking and async APIs. The solders tutorial recommends versioned

In the current solana-py API docs (built from master), AsyncClient.send_transaction takes a solders VersionedTransaction (txn: VersionedTransaction, opts: TxOptsModel | None) and sends bytes(txn) through send_raw_transaction; when opts is None the preflight commitment is the client's commitment. In older releases, passing a solders legacy Transaction produced "AttributeError: 'solders.transaction.Transaction' object has no attribute 'recent_blockhash'" (issue #419, 2024): a solders maintainer said legacy solders Transactions were unsupported there, the repo owner said it should be fixed in 0.3

Two documented bridges connect v1-style code and Kit. @solana/compat converts between legacy and Kit types (fromLegacyPublicKey, fromLegacyKeypair, fromVersionedTransaction; only VersionedTransaction objects convert), and web3.js v3 makes the classes themselves Kit-compatible so a v3 Keypair can be passed wherever Kit wants a signer. The interim @solana/web3-compat shim is superseded: QuickNode says to remove it when moving to v3, and the Solana migration page lists it among earlier packages to migrate away from.

In solders 0.29.0 and earlier, the SendTransaction and SimulateTransaction request builders serialize the transaction as base64 even when no config is given, but JSON-RPC then defaults to base58, so the node rejects the request with 'invalid base58 encoding'. The fix (default to Rpc*Config()) is unreleased in solders main. If you build these requests with solders directly, pass an explicit config with encoding base64 (untested workaround).

solana-py issue #351 (opened 2023-05-02, closed as inactive 2026-06-19) shows 'SignerError: keypair-pubkey mismatch' on a SOL and token transfer, with no confirmed cause or fix. The solders API reference says Transaction.partial_sign fails if a provided signer is not a required signer of the message, and Transaction.sign fails if required signers are missing. Those are the first mistakes to check: a wrong keypair for the fee payer or a missing required signer.

Anza's post-incident response: it removed all users from the @solana and @solana-program npm orgs and moved write access to revocable, granular tokens; it advised any affected team to rotate suspect keys including server keypairs. The attack passed a completed 2FA prompt because the cloned login page captured the one-time code.

Guidance after the compromise: upgrade to 1.95.8 (even when pinned to latest) or downgrade to a version before 1.95.6, and rotate any suspect authority keys, including multisigs, program authorities and server keypairs. Cyfrin added: check yarn.lock or package-lock.json for the bad versions, and keep strict version control and lockfiles.

Both stacks have in-process test validators. solders bundles LiteSVM in every wheel since 0.28.0 as solders.litesvm, which Solana's docs call 'much more convenient and much faster' than solana-test-validator; Kit has @solana/kit-plugin-litesvm (Node only), which replaces the RPC bundle on a client. Either lets a bot's transaction building be exercised without a network.

A fee-bumped rebroadcast is a different transaction. Changing the compute-unit price changes the message, so the message hash and signature change and the AlreadyProcessed check does not link the two. RPC Fast describes rebroadcasting 'with a slightly higher priority fee' when a transaction is not processed within 2 slots. By the official guide's logic both versions can land while the blockhash is valid. Guard such intents on-chain (Circuit added a sequence-enforcer instruction with TTL checks) or accept duplicates.

A commitment mismatch causes false 'Transaction simulation failed: Blockhash not found'. A blockhash fetched at confirmed or processed can be newer than the bank the node uses for simulation and preflight (finalized by default). Fix: use the same commitment for the blockhash fetch and for the simulation or preflight. Solana's sendTransaction docs recommend this 'to avoid confusing behavior'. For simulateTransaction, Helius also advises replaceRecentBlockhash: true, which simulates with a blockhash the node always has.

Solana's docs name @solana/kit the recommended TypeScript SDK. They name @solana/web3.js v3 the recommended web3.js version for teams that are upgrading an existing web3.js app or prefer the class-based API, and they call v3 'the bridge' when a full rewrite to Kit is not practical. The docs call web3.js 1.x legacy: it is in maintenance mode and gets critical fixes only. The web3.js repository README says the same about 1.x and puts new development on v3+.

Anza's root-cause analysis says the phished publisher entered a username and password and completed two-factor authentication on an attacker-run clone of the npm site, so two-factor authentication did not stop the attack.

Solana's official docs (solana-com source at commit 888f1944, 2026-10-20) call @solana/kit 'the recommended TypeScript SDK for building on Solana' and web3.js v3 'the recommended version of web3.js' for anyone upgrading an existing web3.js app or preferring the class-based API. The migration page calls v3 'the bridge' when 'a full rewrite to Kit isn't practical'. Legacy web3.js 1.x is in maintenance mode and gets critical fixes only. Paraphrase of the guidance: new bot, use Kit; existing v1 bot, move to v3 or stay on 1.x.

If the signer path parses as a base58 public key, the CLI builds a signer with no private key that uses presigned signatures supplied separately. Offline signing uses this. `--sign-only` stops the CLI from submitting the transaction. `--blockhash` fixes the blockhash so the signing machine needs no network. The online machine then adds each signature with `--signer PUBKEY=SIGNATURE`. Anza documents this for air-gapped signing devices and multisig, and recommends a durable transaction nonce when signing outlasts the blockhash lifetime (the page says roughly one minute at the time of writing).

Safe retry loop for a bot: (1) fetch the blockhash and lastValidBlockHeight together; (2) sign once; (3) send with maxRetries 0 if the bot owns rebroadcast; (4) rebroadcast the identical signed bytes at an interval while polling getSignatureStatuses; (5) stop when the status shows success or an err; (6) only when block height is above lastValidBlockHeight and a final status lookup is still empty, build a new transaction with a new blockhash. The Solana retry guide, Justin Starry's write-up, the Helius blockhash guide and the fardream library give the same sequence.

Jito tips and Solana priority fees are separate levers: the tip ranks the bundle in the Block Engine auction, the priority fee affects runtime scheduling. Tips do nothing when the leader is not Jito-Solana. For single transactions via Jito sendTransaction, Jito advises setting both a priority fee and a tip; Chainstack suggests a 70/30 split between them.

For single transactions through Jito's sendTransaction, Jito recommends a 70/30 split between priority fee and Jito tip (Chainstack repeats it). Jupiter's Mixed Mode sends one transaction carrying both a tip and a priority fee through the Block Engine and regular RPC at once, landing via whichever is first; the user pays both fees when it lands through Jito and no tip when it lands through RPC.

Routers choose the version, not the bot. Jupiter /build: transactionVersion=1 forces v1 (default '0'). Jupiter /order: maxSupportedTransactionVersion=1 is only a ceiling, so v1 comes back only when Metis wins the route and the order is not gasless. Gasless and auto-sponsored orders are always v0, and the wrong parameter name is silently ignored. DFlow keeps v0 as the default and needs transactionVersion=v1 on /order and /swap. Branch on the version the response reports, and request v1 only for wallets that support it.

Wallets and fee-injection code that prepend Compute Budget instructions at index 0 break durable-nonce transactions, because the runtime only recognises a nonce transaction when AdvanceNonceAccount is instruction 0. A Phantom user reported on devnet that the modified transaction 'can never land'; the thread was closed by redirecting to support with no public fix confirmed.

Encoding trap on reads: Agave v4.3.0 rejects the base58 and binary encodings on getBlock and getTransaction when maxSupportedTransactionVersion is 1 or higher (invalid params: 'base58 encoding is not supported with maxSupportedTransactionVersion >= 1'). The v4.2.0 tag has no such guard. QuickNode likewise says base64 is required alongside the version parameter. On sends, transactions over 1,232 raw bytes must be base64; base58 stays capped at 1,232 raw bytes and larger bodies are rejected with -32602 'too large'.

Lookup tables supply only non-signer accounts. The fee payer and every signer stay in the static key list. Program IDs invoked by top-level instructions must also be static keys, because the v0 sanitizer rejects program ids loaded from lookup tables so programs can be analysed without chain state.

With skipPreflight true, Agave v4.4.0 ignores preflightCommitment and uses processed, and the sendTransaction reference page says the same. The older advice to set preflightCommitment even when skipping preflight no longer changes the node's behaviour.

Do not re-sign with a new blockhash while the first blockhash can still land. The Solana retry guide calls confirming expiry first 'very important' because both transactions can be accepted. Chainstack and the fardream library say the same. The safe order: rebroadcast identical bytes until block height is past lastValidBlockHeight, make a final status lookup, then rebuild.

When `skipPreflight` is true, Agave ignores `preflightCommitment` and selects the bank at `processed` commitment. When `skipPreflight` is false and no `preflightCommitment` is given, the preflight bank uses the default commitment, `finalized`.

On Tuesday 3 December 2024 a spear-phished @solana npm maintainer's credentials let an attacker publish @solana/web3.js 1.95.6 and 1.95.7 with code that sent private key material to the attacker; the window ran from about 3:20pm UTC to 8:25pm UTC, when clean 1.95.8 shipped. It is CVE-2024-54134 / GHSA-jcxm-7wvp-g6p5 (CVSS 4.0 base 8.3, High; affected >=1.95.6 <1.95.8). Impact was limited to projects that directly handle private keys and updated into the window, 'like bots'; non-custodial wallets should not be affected and the Solana protocol was not compromised.

Fetching a blockhash at processed can pick a blockhash from a minority fork that the cluster later abandons. The transaction is then dropped with the blockhash not found. Official docs advise confirmed or finalized when polling getLatestBlockhash. Helius calls confirmed the best practice for sending and states that processed is not recommended for production-critical flows.

Jupiter described a dual-path pattern in Oct 2024: Jito-only mode sends a bundle with a tip to a Jito leader, regular RPC mode relies on priority fees and stake-weighted QoS, and mixed mode sends both so a transaction dropped by an RPC-path leader can still land via Jito. Jupiter says mixed mode costs double the transaction fee when it lands via Jito and pays no Jito tip when it lands via RPC. This is one forum post from 2024 and the product may have changed.

If transactions from your bundle show up on an explorer as individual failed transactions, suspect an uncled block. When a block built by a leader is not accepted by the supermajority, any party that received it can rebroadcast its transactions, and those go through the normal banking stage without bundle atomicity or revert protection. Jito's mitigations are pre- and post-account checks so a rebroadcast is harmless, minimizing leakage, and keeping the tip in the same transaction as the strategy.

Put the tip instruction in the same transaction as the strategy logic with post-transaction checks; if space is short, add slot and balance assertions to a separate tip transaction (Jito's advice). The defence has an Ethereum precedent: Flashbots told users to add a parent-hash check, require(blockhash(block.number - 1) == expectedParentHash), because transactions from an uncled block become visible and targetable ('uncle bandit'); it cited roughly 1 in 20 Ethereum blocks being uncled at the time and the page is marked outdated.

A lookup table holds at most 256 addresses (LOOKUP_TABLE_MAX_ADDRESSES = 256) because entries are addressed by a u8 index. A v0 message references a table by its address plus lists of one-byte indexes for writable and read-only accounts.

A lookup table is an on-chain account that holds at most 256 addresses (LOOKUP_TABLE_MAX_ADDRESSES = 256), because entries are addressed by a u8 index. A v0 message names each table by its address and lists one-byte indexes for the writable and the read-only accounts it loads from that table. ExtendLookupTable fails on a full table, on an extend that would pass 256 entries, and on a deactivated table.

Do not leave throwaway tables open. Tables never expire, and rent stays locked until the authority deactivates the table and later closes it. A bot that creates a table per route leaks rent unless it tracks and closes them. Rent must cover the table when it is created and after each extension. The Solana Foundation saw thousands to tens of thousands of tables created, extended or closed per day, so this churn is normal on mainnet.

When a router quote does not fit, Jupiter's documented fallback is to requote with a lower maxAccounts, starting at 64 and decrementing. In its example, 57 and 56 gave 1,244 bytes and 51 gave 1,213. A lower maxAccounts changes the route and can make it worse or remove it.

RPC transaction responses carry meta.loadedAddresses, with ordered writable and readonly lists, for addresses a v0 transaction loaded from tables. A reader can expand the account list without the table. Decoding a raw v0 message from bytes needs that metadata or the table's state, and vendors report it fails once the table has been closed. v1 avoids this because every account is inline.

A separate trailing tip transaction increases exposure to unbundling after an uncled block (Jito's docs). The community jito-bundle crate does exactly that whenever the bundle has fewer than five transactions, compiling the tip transaction without lookup tables, and appends the tip inline only when the bundle already has five.

A transaction's lifetime is counted in blocks, not seconds. Agave v4.4.0 computes lastValidBlockHeight as block_height + max_processing_age - age, and initialises max_processing_age to MAX_PROCESSING_AGE (150). Because a blockhash's age starts at 0, the Solana docs count 151 blockhashes as recent enough, and the runtime rejects anything older.

Lagging RPC nodes cause false expiry and stale blockhashes. Starry: RPC nodes naturally lag about one block behind the cluster, a node more than 150 slots behind stops serving, and just before that it can return a blockhash that is about to expire. RPC Fast puts shared clusters 2 to 5 slots behind the leader. Fixes the sources give: compare getSlot at processed with getMaxShredInsertSlot, ask several nodes for getLatestBlockhash at confirmed and take the highest context slot, keep resending so a lagging node catches up, and use send-only nodes that do not serve heavy queries such as getProgram

The Block Engine sendTransaction path (https://mainnet.block-engine.jito.wtf/api/v1/transactions) proxies Solana's sendTransaction to the validator with MEV protection on by default and always sets skip_preflight=true, so the RPC does not simulate the transaction first. The query parameter bundleOnly=true sends the transaction only as a single-transaction bundle, which gives revert protection. When the send was made as a bundle, the bundle ID comes back in the x-bundle-id response header.

In March 2024 Telegram trading bots BONKbot (at least about $208,000 per CertiK) and Solareum (about $310,000) lost user funds. The cause was never confirmed; hypotheses were exported-key leakage via another app (BONKbot's claim, disputed by an affected user) and stolen Telegram bot access tokens exposing message history containing keys (Solareum's suggestion). Lesson for bots: never send or store key material where a third-party token can read it.

getRecentPrioritizationFees returns one {slot, prioritizationFee} entry per recent slot, in micro-lamports per CU. It accepts up to 128 account addresses and the node cache holds about 150 recent slots (roughly 1-2 minutes). When accounts are passed, only transactions that locked ALL of them as writable are counted.

In Agave's scheduler ingress only one transaction per durable-nonce account stays queued. A new nonce transaction is dropped if the queued one has priority greater than or equal to its own (or is already scheduled or in flight), and it evicts the queued one only when its priority is strictly higher. Priority is the reward-to-cost ratio, so a fee bump of a pending nonce transaction must raise that ratio, not only the CU price.

@solana/kit ships no dedicated priority-fee setter. The feature request (anza-xyz/kit issue 30, formerly solana-web3.js issue 2123, opened 2024-02-15) was closed as not planned in July 2026 by a stale-issue process. Maintainers had concluded that the generated Compute Budget instruction builders and getComputeUnitEstimateForTransactionMessageFactory already cover the need. Read through a summarizing fetch tool, not the raw page.

A successful sendTransaction response returns only a signature. It does not show that the cluster will process or finalize the transaction. The caller must poll getSignatureStatuses, because the RPC can return a signature for a transaction that is later dropped.

sendTransaction returns only the transaction id (the first signature). A successful response says nothing about whether the cluster will process or finalize the transaction, and the RPC can hand back a signature for a transaction that is later dropped. A bot must poll getSignatureStatuses to learn the outcome.

Underbidding fails quietly: a bundle with too small a tip is accepted but not selected in the auction, so logs show successful submissions while on-chain landing is poor. Size the tip from live data: Jito's REST tip_floor endpoint returns landed-tip percentiles (25th to 99th plus an EMA of the 50th) and a tip_stream websocket pushes updates. Static tips tuned in quiet periods underperform when demand rises.

Because the Block Engine is regional, bots commonly send the same bundle to several regions at once, pre-build and pre-sign during the prior slot, and favor regions near the upcoming leader. Proxies such as Helius expose a jito-region header (ams, dub, fra, lon, nyc, slc, sgp, tyo, mainnet) that geo-routes to the nearest engine if omitted.

A higher priority fee raises ordering priority among transactions the leader already holds. It does not guarantee landing or speed. Chorus One (leader slots 2024-11-18 to 2024-11-25) found fee size had no clear effect on time to inclusion, while stake-weighted QoS cut latency most. Helius (June 2024) found fee-paying transactions land more often and faster than fee-less ones. A Phantom developer said on 2024-03-22 that higher fees did not improve success during meme-coin congestion. OrbitFlare (2026-08-29) says that when transactions never reach the leader, the submission path, not the fee, is

With several accounts the slot value is the maximum of independent per-account minima, so it is a synthetic bound: it can be non-zero even when no landed transaction wrote all the queried accounts, and it can be lower than what a transaction that did write all of them paid. Solana's RPC page and Helius describe the parameter as fees from transactions that lock all of the supplied accounts, which is looser than the implementation.

Agave master has had a load-shedding priority floor since PR 12263 (merged 2026-06-03). When the banking-stage scheduler saturates, it publishes a floor derived from its lowest-priority queued transaction. Sigverify then drops incoming non-vote packets whose priority is at or below the floor, before verifying signatures. Priority is computed from the raw packet bytes with the scheduler's own formula. A low-priority transaction can therefore be dropped at the TPU under load before it is verified.

A higher priority fee does not guarantee inclusion. Helius (Jun 2024) describes the scheduler's guarantee as loose. Phantom's developer-relations manager said on 2024-03-22 that during congestion 'adding a higher fee does not result in improved success rates'. A Feb 2024 analysis argues priority is non-deterministic because scheduler jitter lets cheap transactions land ahead of high-fee ones. The scheduler has changed since these were written (central scheduler default from Agave 2.0, priority floor in 2026).

The Helius Rust SDK sets sig_verify only when signers are supplied, errors out if the simulation returns no unitsConsumed (there is no default CU value), and raises a simulated value below 1000 to 1000.

Inference from these incidents: payloads that run inside the bot process read the key when the program loads it, so `chmod 600`, a separate key file or an environment variable does not stop them. The sources point to controlling which code runs: deep inspection of nested dependencies, stricter CI/CD controls and behavioral detection of post-install anomalies (Socket); verifying that no build used the bad versions (Anza); and rotating keys after exposure. A remote signer keeps the key bytes out of the bot process, though the signer credential stays in it.

A 2025 PyPI campaign monkey-patched key creation. semantic-types (benign when uploaded 22 December 2024, malicious update 26 January 2025) is a hidden dependency of solana-keypair, solana-publickey, solana-mev-agent-py, solana-trading-bot and soltrade. When the retry pool is full, v4.4.0 still broadcasts the batch once and then skips adding the overflow transactions to the pool (counted as retry_queue_overflow). An overflowed transaction therefore gets one send and no rebroadcast. This is a reading of the code, not a documented guarantee.

The node's retry thread stops rebroadcasting a transaction when its message hash appears in the rooted status cache, when the working bank shows it failed, when last_valid_block_height is below the root bank's block height, or when its max_retries count is reached. The expiry test uses the root bank, so a node can keep rebroadcasting after a client's confirmed-level block height has passed lastValidBlockHeight.

Two intentionally identical transactions collide. The duplicate check keys on the whole message hash, so the same fee payer, instructions, accounts and blockhash give AlreadyProcessed on the second send. Change the message (a fresh blockhash or different instruction data) to send a distinct second transaction. Chainstack also warns that transactions can be treated as duplicates when many share a blockhash.

Declare a transaction dead only when both hold: getBlockHeight (the docs say use confirmed) is greater than lastValidBlockHeight, and a status lookup with searchTransactionHistory returns null. While the height is at or below lastValidBlockHeight, a null result means 'not yet', because the transaction may still land.

Lagging RPC nodes cause false drops. If the blockhash comes from one node and the send goes to another, the second may not know the blockhash. The docs advise resending on an interval so the node catches up, keeping time-sensitive sends on dedicated nodes that do not serve heavy queries such as getProgramAccounts, comparing getSlot at processed with getMaxShredInsertSlot, and taking the blockhash from the node with the highest context slot.

Do not use replaceRecentBlockhash true in a simulation that decides whether a signed transaction is still live. The flag swaps in a blockhash that is always valid for simulation, so the simulation passes even when the signed blockhash has expired. LI.FI PR 380 removed the flag from its confirmation path for this reason.

Sandwich mitigation is opt-in: add any pubkey starting with 'jitodontfront' (read-only, need not exist on-chain) to an instruction and the Block Engine rejects any bundle where that transaction is not at index 0 (or contiguous at the front). It only works when the transaction goes through Jito's Block Engine, and Chainstack documents it for mainnet and testnet, not devnet.

Leader-aware timing: because the leader schedule is deterministic, RPC Fast suggests pre-fetching upcoming leaders, pre-building and pre-signing the bundle during the previous slot, and firing at the start of the target slot. A community jito-ts example waits until the next Jito leader is 2 or fewer slots away (getNextScheduledLeader) before it sends.

Query the writable accounts the transaction will lock (pool, vault, user token accounts, oracle), not program IDs. Only writable accounts enter the per-account map, and an empty account list returns only the block-wide minimum. Re-estimate for each transaction from a recent sample, because hot-account fees move within seconds, and apply a hard per-transaction cap. Jupiter likewise advises capping the price and validating it before signing, because estimates can spike when recent blocks hold extreme bids.

When porting a bot to v1, convert a micro-lamport estimate with priorityFeeLamports = ceil(price x computeUnitLimit / 1,000,000), the runtime's own rounding, after clamping the price. Jupiter's v1 builds return an empty computeBudgetInstructions list and a computeUnitPrice for the caller to clamp and convert. Code that scans for Compute Budget instructions to read limits or fees finds nothing on v1 traffic.

Simulation errors leave no on-chain record. Metaplex tells developers to send with `skipPreflight: true` when they need a failing transaction recorded on chain, with its logs visible in an explorer. The failed transaction still pays its fee, so use this for debugging, not as a default.

Loaders reject any input that is not exactly 64 bytes and verify the key halves. Rust (solana-keypair 4.0.1) TryFrom<&[u8]> fails with 'candidate keypair byte array is the wrong length', derives the pubkey from the seed and compares it with constant_time_eq, failing with 'keypair bytes do not specify same pubkey as derived from their secret key'. web3.js 1.98.4 Keypair.fromSecretKey throws 'bad secret key size' unless byteLength is 64 and, unless skipValidation is set, throws 'provided secretKey is invalid' when the recomputed pubkey differs.

Loaders check the length and then recompute the public key. Rust Keypair::try_from(&[u8]) in solana-keypair 4.0.1 fails with 'candidate keypair byte array is the wrong length', derives the public key from the seed, and fails with 'keypair bytes do not specify same pubkey as derived from their secret key'. web3.js 1.98.4 Keypair.fromSecretKey throws 'bad secret key size' unless byteLength is 64, and unless { skipValidation: true } is passed it throws 'provided secretKey is invalid' when the recomputed public key differs. Kora's loaders also reject anything but 64 bytes.

solana-keypair 4.0.1 deliberately does not implement `Clone` for `Keypair`, because 'making a second copy of sensitive secret keys in memory is usually a bad idea'. It offers `insecure_clone` for tests and tells callers to share an `Arc<Keypair>` instead. `TryFrom<&[u8]>` copies the seed into a `Zeroizing` buffer so the temporary copy is wiped once the signing key exists.

A null entry from getSignatureStatuses means 'not found at this commitment', not 'failed'. In current Agave the method reads the status cache of the bank chosen by the request commitment (default processed). With searchTransactionHistory true it then checks rooted ledger history and, if configured, BigTable. Null can mean never landed, dropped, evicted from the cache, or a node without history. Treat a transaction as dead only when block height is past lastValidBlockHeight and a last lookup with history search is also empty. A found status with err set means the transaction landed and failed.

File mode arguments act only when the call creates the file, and the umask can only remove bits. Rust OpenOptionsExt::mode: 'Sets the mode bits that a new file will be created with ... If no mode is set, the default of 0o666 will be used. The operating system masks out bits with the system's umask'. Node fs.writeFile: mode defaults to 0o666 and 'only affects the newly created file'. A Node bot that writes its own key file without { mode: 0o600 } therefore gets 0o666 minus the umask (0o644 under a 022 umask), and passing a mode later does not tighten an existing file.

The simulation result carries err, logs (null when the transaction failed before execution began), unitsConsumed, loadedAccountsDataSize, returnData, replacementBlockhash (when replaceRecentBlockhash is on), fee, preBalances, postBalances, preTokenBalances, postTokenBalances and loadedAddresses. The accounts field returns post-simulation state for the addresses listed in accounts.addresses (no more addresses than the transaction has account keys) and is an array of nulls when err is set. innerInstructions is null unless requested; the docs mark innerInstructionsEncoding as available from Agave

Check size before sending: serialize the built transaction and compare its byte length to 1232 (a serialization RangeError also means too large). Jupiter's documented fallback is to requote with a lower maxAccounts, starting at 64 and decrementing; its example run needed maxAccounts 51 (1213 bytes) after 1244 bytes at 57 and 56. Lower maxAccounts can yield a worse or different route.

To build a v0 swap from a router response, fetch the lookup table accounts the router names, deserialize them into AddressLookupTableAccount objects, and pass them to compileToV0Message. Jupiter's older Metis flow returns addressLookupTableAddresses, and its example loads them with getMultipleAccountsInfo. The Go client needs the same step: decode each table, pass the table map to the transaction builder and set message version v0.

Use your own transaction signatures against your own RPC as the ground truth for 'landed'. Bundle-ID endpoints have short retention (five minutes in flight, recent slots for statuses) and DBI bundles are outside them; keep bundle-status polling for diagnosis only (in-flight state, drop reason). The jito-bundle crate likewise polls both the Jito API and Solana RPC.

Run DBI with a Block Engine fallback. DBI serves BAM leader slots only and pauses while BAM Nodes are in Maintenance Mode. For the Alpenglow transition Jito put all mainnet BAM Nodes into Maintenance Mode, told DBI users to use the legacy Block Engine bundle path, and said Block Engine bundle users, FullSend users and validators needed no action; BAM nodes were to return gradually after activation.

Maker Priority (MPP) and Preconfirmations are not general landing routes. MPP: enrolled market makers send pre-signed price updates to a separate UDP endpoint (PTPU) on each BAM Node; they are scheduled first in every auction batch, need no tip, but must pay at least 1 lamport per compute unit; Jito manages enrollment. Preconfirmations: a read-only stream of transactions a BAM leader has committed to executing, sold through Helius and Triton, with a p50 advantage of 5-10 ms over shred feeds in early tests; they are not finality and exist only for BAM leaders.

Three infrastructure-vendor posts that tune Solana bots attribute latency to the network path, not the SDK, and none compares SDKs. BlockRazor's benchmark (2025-08-26) found end-to-end latency tracked validator concentration (Frankfurt lowest, Tokyo highest), a client-to-server HTTP hop added 20-30 ms in Frankfurt and Tokyo, and a single Tokyo server added 335 ms on average for Frankfurt clients. RPC Fast's copy-trading case study (updated 2026-10-29) used a Rust bot co-located with its node in Frankfurt, Yellowstone gRPC and shred streams, and three parallel landing services. Jito's tip-sizing rule: with sendBundle only the Jito tip matters; with sendTransaction split the total fee roughly 70% priority fee and 30% Jito tip. In high-demand periods the 1,000-lamport minimum may not win the auction, so for sendTransaction set both a priority fee and a larger tip based on current tip-floor percentiles.

On BAM a bundle is signature-checked, then simulated (it advances only if every transaction succeeds), then ranked in a leader-aware auction by total fees (priority fees plus Jito tips) over requested compute units; winners go to the BAM leader as one atomic batch. DBI enforces no minimum tip or priority fee, yet a bundle that pays neither will not land under competition. BAM's auction cadence is derived from slot length and tightens from 25 ms to 20 ms rounds with the 200 ms slots (epoch 1053, 2026-10-09).

Slot time fell to 200 ms at epoch 1053 (2026-10-09, SIMD-0525), per Solana Compass quoting Anza and the solana.com slot-time page. The 150-slot blockhash window is now about 30 seconds, down from 60, and the same 150 slots bound the history that getRecentPrioritizationFees covers. Helius ('roughly 1-2 minutes') and OrbitFlare ('approximately the last minute') still describe the 400 ms-era window. Do not convert slots to time with a fixed 400 ms constant.

For custom retry, set maxRetries to 0, store lastValidBlockHeight from getLatestBlockhash, and rebroadcast the same signed bytes at an interval while getBlockHeight stays at or below it. In v4.4.0 a max_retries of Some(0) makes the node send once and never add the transaction to its retry pool. The official guide accepts exponential backoff or constant-interval resubmission (Mango). RPC Fast advises rebroadcasting every 2 s and polling getSignatureStatuses every 200 ms. A 2026 app (sipher PR 296) runs its resend loop in parallel with confirmation and stops it in a finally block.

Confirm against the signed transaction's own blockhash. LI.FI's SDK polled the lastValidBlockHeight of a fresh getLatestBlockhash call, which is unrelated to the signed transaction, and reported TransactionExpired for swaps that had landed. Its merged fix (PR 448, 2026-08-25) calls isBlockhashValid on the transaction's own blockhash, probes it every 3 s with a three-probe streak, keeps a 5 s minimum and a 90 s ceiling, and ends with a final getSignatureStatuses probe.

Blockhash not found can come from a commitment mismatch. getLatestBlockhash and the sendTransaction preflightCommitment both default to finalized, so a blockhash fetched at confirmed can be newer than the bank that checks it. Use the same commitment for both. Before Alpenglow, finalized trailed confirmed by about 32 slots (13 s), so the mismatch was common. With confirmed and finalized now the same state it should be rare, but a lagging RPC node can still cause it.

Socket (8 January 2025) found npm packages @async-mutex/mutex, dexscreener, solana-transaction-toolkit and solana-stable-web-huks that email private keys passed to them through Gmail SMTP (Nodemailer); the two Solana toolkits also transfer up to 98% of the wallet's lamports to an attacker address. The two Solana packages had 130+ downloads combined. Raw keys handed to a third-party helper package are exposed to that package; Socket advises restricting access to private keys, testing third-party scripts in disposable environments, and monitoring outbound SMTP.

@solana/kit (transaction-confirmation 6.9.0) splits confirmation into racing promises: a block-height exceedence promise that throws SOLANA_ERROR__BLOCK_HEIGHT_EXCEEDED, a nonce-invalidation promise, a recent-signature confirmation promise, and getTimeoutPromise, which throws after 30 s at processed and 60 s otherwise 'when no other heuristic exists'. For a blockhash transaction at 200 ms slots, expiry arrives at about 30 s, so the 60 s timeout is only a backstop.

Vendor-reported usage data: about 62% of v0 transactions reference at least one lookup table, and once converted to v1 half show under 420 bytes of excess and 90% under 1400 (methodology not given). Transactions pulling a few addresses from several tables shrink under v1.

Usage figures are unverified. A developer who sells Solana safety checks reports v1 at 13.8% of non-vote transactions in sampled mainnet blocks the week of 2026-09-14 and 41.9% from 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-30 (44.4% of swaps), with no sampling method. QuickNode reports that about 62% of v0 transactions reference at least one lookup table, and that after conversion to v1 half would show under 420 bytes of excess and 90% under 1,400, with no method given. A negation search found no independent adoption data.

Whether v1 beats v0 with ALTs depends on account count. In a 30-day, 1/16-sample study the Solana Foundation found that half of ALT-using v0 transactions would grow by under 420 bytes as v1 and 90% by under 1,400 bytes, and the converted size distribution thins above about 2,300 to 2,400 bytes. The 64-account cap does not grow, so it may bind for broad multi-pool routes. QuickNode repeats the findings and calls staying on v0 reasonable for account-heavy apps.

About 62% (62.19%) of v0 transactions in that Solana Foundation sample reference at least one ALT. Usage is concentrated: over 350,000 distinct tables appear, yet under 7.5% of them account for 95% of references, and 25 tables account for about 30%. Many tables supply fewer than ten addresses per use. QuickNode repeats the 62% figure from the same report.

One solo developer reports sampling mainnet blocks and finding v1 at 13.8% of non-vote transactions in the week of 2026-09-14 and 41.9% from 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-30 (44.4% of swaps). The post comes from a new account that promotes its own tool, and no independent measurement of v1 share was found.

Durable-nonce transactions follow different expiry rules. Agave's RPC retries them until the nonce account no longer matches the stored nonce value, and adds a fallback deadline of block_height + max_processing_age 'in case of malicious packing of the retry queue'. The runtime accepts a transaction whose blockhash is not among the last 151 only if it is a structurally valid nonce transaction. Do not poll a nonce transaction against the blockhash window. LI.FI's first fix treated the nonce value as a blockhash, which cut its effective window to about 1-2 s.

Direct Bundle Ingest (DBI) lets whitelisted searchers send bundles straight to BAM nodes over QUIC or JSON-RPC, skipping the Block Engine's authenticate, simulate and filter step that added roughly 50 ms. Per Jito's 13 Oct 2026 post, bundles and sendTransaction traffic that still arrive at the Block Engine are now forwarded to BAM through DBI. Access is by request form and Jito publishes no approval criteria.

The IMC measurement (early 2025, about Feb-Jun) saw an average of 14.8M bundles and 26M transactions per day on Jito, with single-transaction bundles the majority and 3-transaction bundles about 2.77% of daily bundles. It found 521,903 sandwich attacks costing victims over $7.7M, and over 86% of single-transaction bundles tipped at or below 100,000 lamports, which the authors read as bundling done only to avoid MEV attacks at a cost of over $2.4M.

Jito states that authenticated Block Engine bundles and sendTransaction traffic are now forwarded to BAM through the DBI pipeline, 'forgoing the Block engine's 50ms auction' (BAM blog, 2026-10-13). The BAM changelog (2026-10-09) says Block Engine bundles are forwarded directly to nearby BAM nodes in every region. The DBI page limits the forwarding to bundles sent to the Block Engine 'from an approved key', so whether unauthenticated default sends get the same path is not stated.

Triton extends getRecentPrioritizationFees with an optional percentile parameter, an integer from 1 to 10,000 (5000 is the median, steps of 0.01%). For each block it returns that percentile of the CU prices paid by non-vote transactions; with account addresses it takes the percentile over the transactions that write-lock each account and returns the highest. Without the parameter it returns the standard minimum.

Do not copy OnFinality's retry example. Its sample catches ExpiredBlockhashError or BlockhashNotFound, fetches a new blockhash and re-signs, without checking whether the first transaction can still land. Its text also says a blockhash expires after about 2 slots (about 1.6 s), which contradicts Agave's 150-block rule.

Alpenglow, the consensus replacement for TowerBFT, was scheduled to activate at epoch 1064 on 21 Oct 2026 (about 14:50 UTC per Anza, about 15:00 UTC per the Solana Foundation). Finality falls to about 150 ms, vote transactions leave blocks so reported TPS drops, and the transaction format and fees do not change. Rotor, which replaces Turbine, has no confirmed date. This is the schedule as of 14 Oct 2026, not confirmation that activation happened.

Agave's commitment levels: processed is the highest slot of the heaviest fork the node processed, with no vote requirement. Confirmed is the highest slot voted on by a supermajority (optimistic confirmation). Finalized is the highest slot at maximum vote lockout. The default level is Finalized, so a request that omits commitment, including the preflight bank of sendTransaction, reads the finalized bank. Before Alpenglow, finalized trailed confirmed by at least 32 slots, about 13 s at 400 ms.

Fetching the blockhash at processed risks a blockhash from a minority fork that the cluster later abandons, and the transaction then fails with Blockhash not found. Under TowerBFT the docs said roughly 5% of blocks were not finalized and recommended confirmed. Helius repeats the 5% figure. No post-Alpenglow fork-drop rate was found.

Treat vendor landing-rate figures as unverified. The RPC Fast and Troop Messenger posts (acceptance 34% to 81%, landing 61% to 94%, tip ceiling 50-70% of expected profit, 50-200 ms ShredStream edge) are from infrastructure vendors selling the remedy; the Troop case is labelled a 'composite' reconstruction and changed several infrastructure variables at once.

Vendor estimators extend the core RPC and differ in semantics. Helius getPriorityFeeEstimate takes a serialized transaction or account keys and returns Min, Low, Medium, High, VeryHigh and UnsafeMax levels; options include recommended, includeAllPriorityFeeLevels and lookbackSlots (1-150, default 150). QuickNode qn_estimatePriorityFees reads up to the last 100 blocks and returns percentiles in 5% steps plus low, medium, high, extreme and recommended. Check what each provider computes before relying on it.

SIMD-0096 (status Activated) pays 100% of the priority fee to the block producer and leaves base-fee distribution unchanged. Before it, 50% of the priority fee was burned (Helius, June 2024; Chorus One, December 2024). The SIMD's drawback section warns that leaders can pay themselves inflated priority fees at little cost, which can make observed fee data overstate the price needed to land.

Provider estimators use different windows and percentile definitions, so a 'high' from one provider is not comparable to another's. Helius getPriorityFeeEstimate takes a serialized transaction or account keys, uses lookbackSlots 1-150 (default 150) and returns min/low/medium/high/veryHigh/unsafeMax without documenting the percentile of each level. QuickNode qn_estimatePriorityFees looks back up to 100 blocks and returns 5% percentiles plus low/medium/high/extreme/recommended, per CU and per transaction. Consumer apps already route through Jito bundles for sandwich protection, which inflates single-transaction bundles. Jupiter's Jito-only mode sends via the Block Engine with a tip (Oct 2024 post); IMC saw Jupiter 'MEV protection' produce a length-one Jito bundle, and found over 86% (864,889,302) of length-one bundles tipped too little to matter for priority (Feb-Jun 2025), about $2.4M spent on such defensive tips.

This run's spot check of api.mainnet-beta.solana.com on 2026-11-06 (solana-core 4.4.0) found getRecentPerformanceSamples at 277 to 286 slots per 60 s, about 210 to 217 ms per slot, and lastValidBlockHeight 149 to 150 blocks above getBlockHeight at confirmed. Circuit Trading's 2024-11-10 postmortem: RPC outages and congestion delayed confirmations, stale position data led the 'fire and forget' trading system to keep issuing orders, and its retry mechanism for expired-blockhash failures resubmitted transactions, some executing up to 700 slots late. The vaults suffered a drawdown of about 20%. Circuit disabled automatic retry on blockhash failures and added a sequence-enforcer instruction with TTL checks. The postmortem does not say whether retries were re-signed with new blockhashes, and no independent coverage was found.

Circuit Trading's own post-mortem of 2024-11-10 blames a drawdown of about 20% in its JLP vaults on RPC outages plus an automatic retry. The system was built for fire-and-forget market making. Delayed confirmations left position data stale, new orders kept being generated without counting in-flight transactions, and the retry re-submitted expired-blockhash transactions, some of which executed up to 700 slots late. Jito-Solana runs on nearly all stake: IMC 2025 reports 97% of the top 500 validators (Sept 2025) and every validator in the highest-staked subset; RPC Fast claims over 95% of active stake. Most leaders are therefore Jito leaders, but a bundle sent when the next leader is not Jito still drops.

Jito's docs (page updated 2026-11-05) say the Block Engine's parallel auctions run at 50 ms ticks. Jito's 13 Oct 2026 Direct Bundle Ingest post, as relayed by Solana Compass, also refers to the Block Engine's 50 ms auction and to an extra hop of roughly 50 ms on the Block Engine route into BAM.

Solana's slot-time target dropped to 200 ms at epoch 1053 on 9 Oct 2026, and BAM's auction cadence, which is derived from slot length, tightened from 25 ms to 20 ms. The RPC Fast guide (updated 2026-09-07) and the IMC paper still describe 400 ms slots, so slot-timing advice written before 9 Oct 2026 has about half the time budget it assumed. Both news sources relay Jito's BAM changelog.

BAM (Block Assembly Marketplace) went live on Solana mainnet on 2025-09-25. Jito's 9 Oct 2026 changelog, as relayed by Solana Compass and Crypto Briefing, put BAM at 385 connected validators and 164 million SOL, which is 37% of network stake at epoch 1050. The two outlets share one origin (Jito), so the adoption figures count as one vendor source.

Scale landing expectations against Jito's own network-wide numbers. For 2026-09-03 to 09-20 and 09-20 to 10-07, BAM received 23.76B then 21.97B unique bundles and landed 106.3M then 124.3M, an end-to-end land rate of 0.45% then 0.57% (about 1 in 175). Simulation success was 11.43% then 16.14%, auction success 3.4% then 4.7%, and failed simulations used 50% then 41% of compute. The figures come from Jito, mix DBI with Block Engine flow, and cover only the first weeks of the new pipeline.

Anza's post on SetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit says that without the instruction a transaction is charged for loading up to 64 MB of account data at 8 CUs per 32 KB (about 16,000 CUs), and that requesting only the bytes needed lowers total CUs and so raises priority without changing the fee. Its worked token-transfer example moves the priority score from 0.30 to 0.63. The example halves the priority fee inside the reward, which predates SIMD-0096, so treat the numbers as illustration only.

The 150-block window was about 60 seconds at 400 ms slots. SIMD-0525 cut slot time in four steps to 200 ms, which went live on mainnet at epoch 1053 on 2026-10-09, so the same window now covers about 30 seconds of history. Vendor guides that call the window '1-2 minutes' predate this change, and code should not multiply slot counts by 400 ms to get elapsed time.

A passing simulation does not bind the landing result, because state-dependent errors dominate landed Solana failures. The ISSTA 2025 study of failed on-chain transactions (data window 2023-08-01 to 2024-07-31) finds that 'price or profit not met' and 'invalid status' errors make up 67.18% of failures in arXiv v1 and 86.4% in the ISSTA program abstract. The authors tie price-or-profit-not-met to arbitrage bots on Jupiter V6 when expected profit does not materialize or conditions change during execution, and invalid-status errors to sniper bots on Raydium. The paper does not mention simulation

Two typosquatted Rust crates, `faster_log` and `async_println` (both published 2025-05-25; 7,181 and 1,243 downloads), searched the files they processed for quoted Ethereum private keys (0x plus 64 hex characters), Solana-style Base58 secrets and bracketed byte arrays, and posted matches to `mainnet[.]solana-rpc-pool[.]workers[.]dev`. The code ran at runtime, not at build time. crates.io deleted the crates at 15:34 UTC on 2025-09-24 after Socket's report. Inference: these patterns match a keypair stored as a JSON array (the `id.json` shape) or as a base58 string in a scanned file.

Measurement study (Northeastern, IMC 2025, four months of early-2025 data): Jito bundles are still used for sandwiching (over 500K attacks, over $7.7M victim losses), and over 86% of single-transaction bundles carried tips too low for priority placement, i.e. people bundle only to hide from sandwiches, spending over $2.4M in tips. Bundle contents are not visible on the final ledger, so the authors scraped the undocumented Jito Explorer API.

Confirmed is a conditional guarantee, not finality. Anza's optimistic-confirmation proposal says applications can assume that 2/3+ votes observed in gossip confirm a block, and that otherwise at least 4.66% of the network is violating the protocol. It sets safety at 1/3+X with X = 4.66% slashable stake, and plans no automatic slashing at first (stake is frozen in the next epoch after a violation). Starry says confirmed blocks can be rolled back only if a small share of stake does slashable things, and that this has never happened. Helius reports no confirmed block has reverted. Teams add a margin to simulated `unitsConsumed`. Solana's compute guide gives +10% as its example, Helius's TypeScript docs use `Math.ceil(units * 1.1)`, and Chainstack uses `ceil(units * 1.1)` inside a stated 10-20% range. The Helius Rust SDK instead defaults to a 1.25 multiplier (25%) and raises any simulated value below 1000 to 1000.

Simulated compute use is an estimate, not a bound. The web3.js estimator warns that real consumption 'might be higher or lower' than the simulation. Solana's guide says compute use is not always stable, for example when a program calls `find_program_address`, and offers two fixes: test over time to find the ceiling, or add a percentage to the simulated value. The Helius Rust SDK cites 'simulation environment differences' and 'worst-case execution paths' for its 25% buffer.

Commitment levels: processed means a leader included the transaction in a block; confirmed means a supermajority (66% or more of stake) voted on the block; finalized means about 31 further blocks sit on it and it is effectively irreversible. Helius reports no confirmed block has ever reverted, but that is a vendor claim and confirmed is not formally final.

The 150 ms finality figure is an expectation, not a constant. The Solana page says it was measured against the stake distribution at test time and varies with whether a block finalizes in one voting round or two. Solana Compass noted the figure is Anza's own and that no independent post-switch measurement existed at publication. This run found no independent mainnet measurement either.

After Alpenglow, confirmed and finalized point at the same certificate-backed block. SIMD-0326 says optimistic confirmation is 'superseded by faster (actual) finality'. Chainstack's migration guide says confirmed keeps working but will be removed in a later release, and that the getSignatureStatuses confirmations field stays 0 until the transaction is final, then becomes null. A 2026-11-06 sample of public mainnet RPC found processed, confirmed and finalized slots within 0 to 2 slots of each other (finalized was sometimes ahead of confirmed), against the pre-Alpenglow gap of about 32 slots. Under Alpenglow, Chainstack advises replacing status polling with signatureSubscribe push notifications and warns that caches with a TTL above about 250 ms can serve stale data once finality is near-instant. This is single-vendor guidance and its finality numbers are targets that were not yet measured on mainnet when it was written.

RPC Fast advertises its pre-block streaming simulator as '~95% execution agreement' with '~800 us median overhead', but the page defines neither the metric nor the sample. Treat the figure as marketing, not as a measured pass-to-landing rate.

Commitment guidance changed with Alpenglow. The Solana docs say to point new code at finalized, because it now arrives in about 150 ms, and to re-check every timeout, retry or UX delay tuned to 12.8-second finality. They say confirmed will be removed in a later release. Triton One warns not to move to finalized before the node runs Alpenglow, or requests wait the old 12.8 s.

RPCFast sells a simulator that runs inside its shred stream and advertises '~95% execution agreement' and a '~800 microsecond median overhead'. The page gives no method, sample size, date, or comparison to RPC simulateTransaction, so treat both figures as unverified marketing.

The Python build-and-sign flow is MessageV0.try_compile(payer, instructions, address_lookup_table_accounts, recent_blockhash) then VersionedTransaction(message, [keypair]); the solders tutorial says to use versioned transactions 'if you have a choice' and leaves blockhash fetching and sending to solana-py. The Kit flow is a pipe of pure transforms (createTransactionMessage({version: 0}), setTransactionMessageFeePayer, setTransactionMessageLifetimeUsingBlockhash). TypeScript checks it at author time: a missing fee payer, a missing lifetime or an unsigned send is a type error, not an RPC error.

Building and signing v1 needs newer SDKs than reading it. Jupiter: build, deserialize and sign v1 with @solana/kit v8 or later; @solana/web3.js v1 cannot sign v1 transactions; not every wallet extension can sign v1. Helius lists @solana/kit 8.0, @solana/web3.js v3 and Rust crates built on Agave 4.2. QuickNode (2026-09-01) lists solders 0.29.0 and solana-go 1.23.0 as read and send, and web3.js 1.99.0 as read only.

The error string 'SignerError: keypair-pubkey mismatch' appears in a 2023 solana-py issue thread: the poster signed with a freshly created Keypair() that was not the key of any required signer, and a commenter's diagnosis was that the keypair passed to sign() must be the actual wallet key matching the signer pubkey in the message. The code in the thread used the old solana.transaction.Transaction API, so treat it as a symptom pointer, not a fix for current releases.

Kit now has a plugin-composed client. Solana's docs build it as createClient().use(signer(payer)).use(solanaMainnetRpc()) with plugins from @solana/kit-plugin-signer and @solana/kit-plugin-rpc; client.sendTransaction([...]) then 'resolves the blockhash, estimates compute, signs with the client's payer, and submits', throws if the plan does not fit one transaction (sendTransactions handles batches), and the mainnet preset makes airdrop a compile-time error. The plugins are pre-1.0 (kit-plugin-rpc 0.23.0 requires @solana/kit ^8.6.0), and the docs page still says 'Kit is v7+' and 'plugin packages

Kit builds transactions as a pipe of pure transforms (createTransactionMessage, then setTransactionMessageFeePayer, setTransactionMessageLifetimeUsingBlockhash and instruction appenders). The transform functions freeze the message object so it cannot be mutated in place, and TypeScript raises a type error for a missing fee payer, blockhash lifetime or signature. Signing uses signer objects from @solana/signers such as generateKeyPairSigner.

A v1 sender must set the compute unit limit and the loaded-accounts data size limit explicitly: v1 defaults both to zero, so a transaction that omits them fails. ComputeBudget program instructions are ignored in v1 (they run as successful no-ops and still use compute units). The priority fee in v1 is a total in lamports. The sibling concept on compute budget owns the details.

Solana's official docs tell new apps to build directly on @solana/kit and present web3.js v3 only as a legacy-interop bridge for large v1 codebases that cannot be rewritten yet. v3 keeps the class names Connection, Keypair, Transaction and PublicKey but runs on Kit internals.

To move an ALT-based builder to v1, resolve each table entry, put the addresses inline in the single address array, and deduplicate them, because v1 rejects duplicates. Stay within 64 addresses and 4,096 bytes. Send transactions over 1,232 raw bytes as base64, since base58 stays capped at 1,232. v1 also defaults the compute-unit limit and loaded-accounts-data limit to zero, so set both explicitly (the compute-budget concept covers how).

Kit's live README is stale against its own releases. It still documents estimateComputeUnitLimitFactory in its compute-unit section (the README was last edited 2026-10-27), but Kit v8.0.0 (2026-08-21) removed that factory and estimateAndSetComputeUnitLimitFactory in favor of estimateResourceLimitsFactory and estimateAndSetResourceLimitsFactory, which also set the loaded-accounts-data-size limit for v1 transactions. Snippets copied from the README can fail on Kit 8.

bigint pitfalls after the v3 upgrade: arithmetic that mixes a bigint RPC value with a number throws 'TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types'; JSON.stringify on an RPC result throws 'Do not know how to serialize a BigInt' unless given a replacer; send options such as maxRetries are typed bigint, so maxRetries: 0 fails to compile and must be written 0n; a lamport balance above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (about 9 million SOL) loses precision if converted to number. Keep bigint through application state and convert only at display or API boundaries.

Rebroadcasting identical signed bytes cannot execute twice. Agave's check_transactions rejects a message hash that is already in the StatusCache with AlreadyProcessed ('This transaction has already been processed'). The cost is an error, not a double spend. With preflight on, sendTransaction runs a simulation and returns any simulation error, so a Drift keeper-bot log shows 'Transaction simulation failed: This transaction has already been processed'. A rebroadcast loop must treat that error as 'look up the signature', not as failure. Re-sending with skipPreflight true, as the Solana guide's ex

A transaction that fails on chain still costs the fee. Solana's fee docs say the total fee (5,000 lamports per signature plus the priority fee) is deducted before execution and is charged whether the transaction succeeds or fails. A failure caught by preflight costs nothing, because the node rejects it before forwarding. With skipPreflight true, every deterministic error that preflight would have caught is paid for if the transaction lands. The retry guide titles this 'The Cost of Skipping Preflight'.

Limits the Anza proposal lists for v0 lookups: signers cannot be loaded through a table (full signer addresses stay in the message); hardware wallets cannot show details of accounts referenced through a table; only single-level lookups work; and a transaction may not load the same account twice, whether through account_keys or through a table.

Transaction simulation failed: Blockhash not found` (RPC error -32002 on preflight, or `err: 'BlockhashNotFound'` in a plain simulation) means the node cannot find the transaction's blockhash. Helius lists three causes: a blockhash that is too old, a blockhash newer than the one the node checks against (for example fetched at `confirmed` but checked at `finalized`), and a lagging or different RPC node. For simulation set `replaceRecentBlockhash: true`; for sends match `preflightCommitment` to the commitment used to fetch the blockhash.

@solana/kit 6.9.0 estimateComputeUnitLimitFactory sets the CU limit to 1,400,000 before it simulates, simulates with sigVerify false, replaces the blockhash unless the message uses a durable nonce, and returns unitsConsumed capped at u32 max. It adds no margin; its docs suggest wrapping it to multiply the estimate by about 1.1. estimateAndSetComputeUnitLimitFactory leaves a message unchanged when its limit is already set to a value other than 0 or 1,400,000. The earlier web3.js PR 2703 also says the estimate may be higher or lower than real use and advises a fixed or multiplicative buffer.

Transactions over 1232 raw bytes must be sent base64-encoded; base58 submission stays capped at 1232 raw bytes. V1 senders must also set compute unit limit and loaded-accounts data size explicitly, because v1 defaults them to zero.

Jupiter's Swap API serves v1 only on request (announced 2026-10-07). On /build, transactionVersion=1 forces v1. On /order, maxSupportedTransactionVersion=1 is only a ceiling: you get v1 only when the Metis router wins and the order is not gasless, otherwise v0, so read the response transactionVersion. The two parameter names are not interchangeable, and the wrong one is silently ignored. Under v1, /build returns empty computeBudgetInstructions, an empty addressesByLookupTableAddress and a computeUnitPrice field; the integrator sets the compute unit limit, loaded-accounts data size limit and pr

The priority fee is ceil(SetComputeUnitPrice x SetComputeUnitLimit / 1,000,000) lamports, where the price is in micro-lamports per CU. It is charged on the requested CU limit, not on the CUs the transaction actually consumes, so a default or oversized limit means paying for compute that never runs.

The priority fee is charged on the requested compute-unit limit, not on `unitsConsumed`: fee = ceil(SetComputeUnitPrice x SetComputeUnitLimit / 1,000,000). Without a `SetComputeUnitLimit` instruction the default budget is 200,000 CU per non-builtin instruction and 3,000 per builtin, capped at 1,400,000, so an unsized transaction usually reserves more than it uses. This is the main reason bots simulate before they send.

A dry-run simulation needs no private key and no fresh blockhash. The docs say the transaction need not be signed unless sigVerify is true, and replaceRecentBlockhash: true substitutes a valid blockhash; Helius's example simulates its compute-unit test transaction this way (replaceRecentBlockhash: true, sigVerify: false). Limit: with sigVerify false the simulation cannot catch missing or invalid signatures; only the send-time preflight verifies them. A bot can therefore simulate unsigned and sign only after it decides to send.

Other Kit major changes that break bot-facing code: v3.0.0 requires a SendableTransaction (fully signed and within the size limit) before the send helpers and removed getComputeUnitEstimateForTransactionMessageFactory; v6.0.0 changed the createTransactionPlanExecutor callback executeTransactionMessage to (context, message, config); v8.0.0 stopped writing to the execution context in createTransactionPlanExecutor.

A February 2025 PythonAnywhere thread (Python 3.9; solana-py 0.26.0, 0.36.5, 0.36.6; solders 0.24 to 0.26) shows the cost of trial-and-error version mixing: "TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'proxy'" from Client(...), "No matching distribution found" for some solders releases, and .sign or .create_signatures missing depending on the solders release. The only reply blamed an LLM-suggested API and told the poster to read the package docs; the cause stayed unresolved. Today solders 0.28.0 requires Python 3.10+ and solana-py 0.37.1 dropped Python 3.9, so an old interpreter

After the incident Anza removed all users from the @solana and @solana-program npm organizations and moved write access to revocable, granular access tokens. Timeline per Anza: 1.95.6 was deprecated at 19:39 UTC and 1.95.7 at 20:52 UTC on 2024-12-03, and npm staff removed both by about 00:22 UTC on 2024-12-04.

Inference: Kit's lack of third-party dependencies shrinks the transitive attack surface but not the publish-account risk, because Kit packages ship under the same @solana npm namespace whose publish access was phished in 2024. Treat any SDK upgrade as a code-change event for a key-holding bot: pin exact versions, install from a lockfile, and review the diff of key-handling methods before deploying.

npm's latest dist-tag decides what a bare install fetches. On 2026-10-06 npm latest was still 1.99.0 and next was 3.0.1, so 'npm install @solana/web3.js' returned v1; the v3.0.0 release notes said 3.x would move from next to latest on October 19. As of 2026-11-06 latest is 3.1.1, and the Solana docs (commit 888f1944, 2026-10-20) dropped the '@3' install tag and pinned legacy to '@1'. A fresh install, or a 'latest' or '*' range, therefore now crosses the v1-to-v3 break. By semver caret rules a '^1.x' range cannot select 3.x (inference; not stated in the sources).
