The minimum tip depends on the path. Jito Block Engine docs: 1,000 lamports (the IMC study measured the same floor in Feb-Jun 2025, and a 2025 error string reads 'Bundle must tip at least 1000 lamports'). DBI: no minimum. QuickNode: 'Jito no longer provides a minimum tip for bundles'. Helius basic bundles: 5,000 lamports; Helius Sender: 0.001 SOL for Sender Max or 0.000005 SOL for SWQOS-only. FullSend: a per-transaction tip set by your TPS tier.

Literal errors and causes: 'Bundle must tip at least 1000 lamports' (tip undefined or zero on the Block Engine, 2025 reports); 'Bundle Dropped, no connected leader up soon' (no Jito leader upcoming, matching bundle.proto DroppedBundle 'e.g. because no leader upcoming'); 'Error: 7 PERMISSION_DENIED: The supplied pubkey is not authorized to generate a token' (a searcher client still passing an auth keypair; Jito's docs say default sends need no key, so pass null or None).

Block Engine sendBundle (JSON-RPC POST /api/v1/bundles) takes up to five fully signed transactions and returns a bundle_id, the SHA-256 hash of the transaction signatures, on acceptance only. The encoding option defaults to base58 (slow, deprecated), so pass {'encoding': 'base64'} explicitly when sending base64 strings. sendTransaction on /api/v1/transactions proxies to the validator, always sets skip_preflight=true, and with ?bundleOnly=true goes out only as a one-transaction bundle for revert protection; the bundle ID then arrives in the x-bundle-id response header.

With `skipPreflight: false`, Agave v4.4.1 `sendTransaction` verifies signatures, runs a node-health check (unless the operator disabled it), then calls `simulate_transaction(&tx, false)` on the preflight bank. A failed simulation returns RPC error -32002 with the message `Transaction simulation failed: <err>` and the simulation result as `data`; an unhealthy node returns -32005 `Node is behind by N slots`. With `skipPreflight: true` the node skips all three steps.

With skipPreflight false, sendTransaction's preflight runs in this order: signature verification, a node-health check, then the same simulation at preflightCommitment (default finalized). If the node is behind, it returns NodeUnhealthy (-32005) before simulating, unless the node was started with skip_preflight_health_check. If the simulation fails, it returns error -32002 with the message 'Transaction simulation failed: <TransactionError>' and the simulation result (logs, unitsConsumed, returnData, loadedAccountsDataSize, fee) as error data; the preflight copy has no accounts or innerInstructi

An oversize transaction shows up as 'Transaction too large: XXXX > 1232' (Chainstack), as a send error such as 'base64 encoded solana_sdk::transaction::versioned::VersionedTransaction too large: 1964 bytes (max: encoded/raw 1644/1232)' (solana-go issue 173), or as a RangeError while serializing in web3.js (Jupiter's example). Serialize the built transaction and compare its length to 1232 before sending.

The -32015 error predates V1. Koinly users hit 'Transaction version (0) is not supported by the requesting client' when syncing Solana wallets (reports from 2022-11-10; fixed 2023-01-26; 76 votes), and a Rust client user in 2024-04-19 found no way to pass maxSupportedTransactionVersion through get_transaction. Products that ignore versioned transactions fail the same way after V1.

Check size before signing. Serialize the built transaction and compare its length with 1,232; a RangeError during serialization also means it is too large. Oversize transactions fail with messages such as 'Transaction too large: XXXX > 1232' or, from the Rust RPC client, 'VersionedTransaction too large: 1964 bytes (max: encoded/raw 1644/1232)'.

Leaving out the router's tables inflates a swap past the limit. In solana-go issue 173 (opened 2024-02-14, still open), a Jupiter swap built without the tables failed with a 1,964-byte 'VersionedTransaction too large' error against the 1,232 limit. A commenter on 2025-12-21 reported the fix: fetch each addressLookupTableAddresses account, decode it, pass the table map to the builder and set message version v0. No maintainer confirmed the cause.

FullSend pricing as documented on 2026-11-05: every transaction must carry a tip to a FullSend tip address sized by the account's TPS limit (5 TPS: 1,000,000 lamports; 10 TPS: 100,000; 25 TPS: 10,000), the tip is conditional on successful execution, and a transaction without the tip is dropped. The regional direct endpoints (ewr1, fra1, tyo1 on port 8443) use self-signed TLS and need client-side failover with a recommended 1,000 ms timeout. Jito's '100% land rates' wording is a vendor claim with no published measurement behind it.

FullSend pricing is a per-transaction tip set by your TPS rate-limit tier: 5 TPS = 1,000,000 lamports, 10 TPS = 100,000, 25 TPS = 10,000, paid to FullSend tip addresses issued on access. The tip is conditional on successful execution, and a transaction without it is dropped. The page claims '100% land rates' and gives no method.

At a 30-second window, a slow signer eats the budget. Solana's slot-time page warns that offline and human-approval flows now have less slack. The docs advise fetching the blockhash right before signing, polling so a fresh one is ready, and replacing a transaction's blockhash just before a wallet signs. A bot with a remote signer, HSM or approval step should budget that round trip inside the 30 s.

The @solana/kit estimator sets the message's limit to 1,400,000 before simulating so the simulation cannot fail on CU exhaustion, then downcasts unitsConsumed (u64) to a number capped at u32 max (4,294,967,295) because SetComputeUnitLimit takes a u32. It throws if unitsConsumed is missing or the simulation errors, and does not add a buffer itself; callers wrap it to pad.

Lookup tables are a v0-only feature. A legacy transaction cannot use them, and the message must be compiled as v0 (for example compileToV0Message([lookupTableAccount]) in web3.js) for the runtime to resolve indexes from the table.

Stale consumers and nodes can misread v1 without raising an error. QuickNode says streaming consumers cannot declare v1 support: an older Yellowstone geyser plugin downgrades v1 to v0 with an empty compute budget, so it asks for plugin 15.1.1 and protobuf stubs 12.6.0 or later (which add Message.config). Solana Compass says RPC nodes need Agave 4.2.2 or later so v1 messages are not stored as v0 with zeroed compute budgets. QuickNode also warns to test for v1 before the generic 'versioned' check, because versioned is true for both v0 and v1.

Derived from three constants: the 512-entry cool-down is longer than the 150-slot blockhash lifetime. A transaction built while its table was fully active therefore cannot lose that table to deactivate-then-close before its blockhash expires. A table that is already deactivating at build time has no such guarantee. estimate_last_valid_slot returns deactivation_slot + 512; while the current slot is below that value the table is certainly still usable, and skipped slots can make the estimate loose.

Reads of full transactions must pass maxSupportedTransactionVersion as the JSON integer 1. If the parameter is omitted, getTransaction returns only legacy transactions and any versioned one raises an error. A value of 0 fails on a v1 transaction exactly like omission, and the string '1' fails with -32602. One v1 transaction fails an entire getBlock with -32015, and blockSubscribe emits block: null and stops advancing. getSignaturesForAddress never inspects bodies, so it is unaffected.

Never put a Jito tip account in an address lookup table. Jito warns that tips must not use lookup tables, the jito-bundle crate validates this up front because a lookup table that contains a tip account makes the transaction fail at runtime, and Solana's dontfront guide repeats the rule (the dontfront account itself may be loaded through a table).

Transaction v1 (SIMD-0385) activated on mainnet at the first slot of epoch 1035 (slot 447,120,000, about 01:04 UTC on 2026-09-15). A v1 message carries the compute unit limit, loaded-accounts data size limit, heap size and priority fee in a transaction config, and the priority fee is a total in lamports, not micro-lamports per CU. Compute Budget instructions in a v1 transaction are ignored for configuration but still run as no-ops that cost 150 CUs each. Unset values default to 0, so a v1 transaction without a CU limit fails. The v1 fee is 5,000 x required signatures + priorityFee. Legacy and

sendTransaction's default preflight does two checks: signature verification, then a simulation against the bank state at preflightCommitment. A failing preflight returns the same error structure as simulateTransaction (err, logs, unitsConsumed). Setting skipPreflight: true skips both checks.

Agave returns MinContextSlotNotReached when the serving bank's slot is below the request's minContextSlot. Current code accepts the field on sendTransaction, getLatestBlockhash, isBlockhashValid and getSignatureStatuses. Passing the context slot of the blockhash response turns a silent read from a lagging node into an explicit error. No guide in this pass recommends the pattern, so treat it as an inference from the code.
Jito's JSON-RPC defaults to base58 transaction encoding, but base58 is deprecated and slow. Send base64 and set the encoding option to base64 explicitly on every sendBundle and sendTransaction call.

Compute Budget instruction rules per Chainstack: only one of each instruction variant is allowed per transaction; duplicates produce a DuplicateInstruction error and the transaction fails. SetComputeUnitLimit accepts any u32 but is clamped to 1,400,000, and SetComputeUnitPrice accepts any u64.

The priority fee is ceil(compute_unit_price * compute_unit_limit / 1,000,000) lamports, where the price is in micro-lamports per CU. The limit in the formula is the requested (or default) CU limit, not the CUs the transaction consumes, so the transaction pays for requested units it never uses. Agave's get_prioritization_fee rounds up and saturates at u64::MAX. A transaction with no SetComputeUnitPrice has price 0 and pays no priority fee.

With no SetComputeUnitLimit instruction, Agave sets the limit to 3,000 CUs per builtin instruction plus 200,000 CUs per non-builtin instruction (a builtin that has migrated to SBF counts as 200,000), clamped to 1,400,000. Compute Budget instructions are themselves builtin instructions and count in the sum, so a SOL transfer plus a lone SetComputeUnitPrice gets 6,000 CUs. SIMD-0170 (status Activated) warns that transactions relying on this default can start failing and should set the limit explicitly.

The Compute Budget Program has four instructions: RequestHeapFrame, SetComputeUnitLimit, SetComputeUnitPrice and SetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit. A second instruction of the same variant fails the whole transaction with TransactionError::DuplicateInstruction(index). SetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit of 0 fails with InvalidLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit (larger values are clamped to 64 MiB). A heap size outside 32-256 KiB or not a multiple of 1,024, and any Compute Budget instruction data that does not decode, fail with InstructionError::InvalidInstructionData.

The sources support this bot loop: (1) build the transaction with a 1,400,000-unit placeholder limit and the intended priority price; (2) simulate with `replaceRecentBlockhash: true`, `sigVerify: false`, the commitment you will send at, and `minContextSlot` when state depends on a prior transaction; (3) stop if `err` is non-null; (4) rebuild with `unitsConsumed` plus a margin and a real blockhash fetched at `confirmed` or higher; (5) sign and send, using `skipPreflight` only when latency outweighs the cost of failed landings. Simulation, and so preflight, applies a stricter blockhash age limit than the leader. Agave runs simulation with max age MAX_PROCESSING_AGE minus MAX_TRANSACTION_FORWARDING_DELAY, which is 150 minus 6, so 144 blocks, because the transaction must still be valid after it is forwarded. The leader accepts 150. A blockhash 145 to 150 blocks old therefore fails simulation with BlockhashNotFound although it could still land. Solana's retry guide rounds the preflight limit to 'within the last 150 blocks'.

Phantom adds priority fees at signing time for signTransaction, signAllTransactions and signAndSendTransaction, but only when the transaction has no signatures, has no existing priority-fee instructions, and stays under 1,232 bytes after the addition. Its docs discourage dapps from setting their own fees and do not say where Phantom places the instructions. For unsigned transactions that a wallet will sign, the web3.js authors suggest leaving the CU limit to the wallet, which may estimate better.

V1 does not support address lookup tables: a v1 message has no addressTableLookups field, and every account is an inline 32-byte key (up to 64 addresses, 2048 bytes). V1 raises the raw size limit from 1232 to 4096 bytes. A v1 transaction starts with version byte 0x81 and carries its signatures at the end. An app migrating from v0 resolves its table entries and inlines the addresses.
V1 keeps the per-transaction caps at 12 signatures, 64 instructions and 64 account addresses (255 account indexes per instruction); only the byte limit grows.

The runtime limit for legacy and v0 transactions is 64 account locks, even with lookup tables. The Anza v0 proposal's 'max of 256 unique accounts' is only the u8 index ceiling. SIMD-0596 says legacy and v0 'MUST remain limited to 64 account locks', SIMD-0385's constraint table lists 64 as the prior maximum, Helius says tables let a transaction reach 'the runtime's 64-account limit', and Jupiter says v0 and v1 'both cap at 64 accounts'.

V1 has no address lookup tables: SIMD-0385 says the format 'notably does not include address lookup tables'. Every account is a full 32-byte key inline, up to 64 (2,048 bytes). The limit is 4,096 bytes (SIMD-0385's own constraint table sets it; SIMD-0296 gives the rationale). The first byte is 129 (0x81), signatures move to the end, and the caps stay at 12 signatures, 64 instructions and 255 accounts per instruction. The format could carry up to 96 addresses, but the runtime caps v1 at 64.

Do not catch -32015 and report 'transaction not found'. Helius says that seeing -32015 in logs means the project is already failing on versioned transactions. One developer reports that batch reads (getParsedTransactions, getTransactions) throw for the whole batch when one entry is v1, hiding the other 49 transactions, and that apps returning null on the error mark paid transactions as missing. Older guides hard-code the old setting: OnFinality's lookup-table guide (undated) uses maxSupportedTransactionVersion 0 only, which now fails on v1 data.

A v1 message has no address-table field. Every account is an inline 32-byte key, up to 64 addresses (2,048 bytes). v1 raises only the byte limit, to 4,096; signatures stay at 12, instructions at 64 and accounts per instruction at 255. SIMD-0385 calls ALTs 'a significant source of complexity for validators', and the Solana docs call their removal deliberate.

The failure is JSON-RPC code -32015, with a message like 'Transaction version (0) is not supported by the requesting client. Please try the request again with the following configuration parameter: "maxSupportedTransactionVersion": 0'. The same text hit Koinly's Solana sync in 2022-23 and a Rust-client user in 2024 whose helper could not set the parameter. Helius's v1 sample words the tail differently. Match on code -32015 and the phrase 'is not supported by the requesting client', not the whole string.

With preflight enabled, sendTransaction simulates against the bank at preflightCommitment (default finalized) and returns the simulation error, for example 'Transaction simulation failed: Blockhash not found', if that bank does not know the blockhash. Before Alpenglow, a blockhash fetched at confirmed could be newer than the finalized bank, so the guides say to set preflightCommitment to the commitment used to fetch the blockhash. The mismatch matters less now that finalized and confirmed are within 0 to 2 slots, but setting the value explicitly is still cheap.

A reported web3.js case: a transaction sent with a confirmed blockhash was already finalized, yet connection.confirmTransaction threw the block-height-exceeded expiry error. The issue was closed by moving the report to the Agave repository, with no root cause given. Bots should verify the signature status before treating an expiry exception as proof the transaction failed.

One web3.js user reported confirmTransaction throwing the block-height-exceeded error for a transaction that had already finalized, after sending with a confirmed blockhash and confirming at confirmed. The issue tracker bot closed it by pointing to the Agave repo, and no cause was recorded. Treat an expiry exception as a prompt to check the signature status before rebuilding.

The Block Engine runs parallel auctions. Bundles whose account-lock patterns intersect on a writable account ((w,w), (r,w) or (w,r)) compete in one auction; bundles that do not intersect, or that overlap only on reads, run in separate auctions. Within an auction bundles are ranked by requested tip per requested compute unit, and Jito submits the highest-paying combination to the validator up to a compute-unit limit.

Chorus One measured inclusion times in its own validator's slots (18-25 Nov 2024, no sample size published) and found that Jito tip size and priority-fee size had no clear effect on time to inclusion, while senders on stake-weighted QoS connections landed faster, especially slow users. The IMC paper relays this study (its reference 1) for length-one bundles, so the two count as one source. It scopes the claim that a bigger tip lands faster: a tip buys rank in a contended auction, and this study did not isolate that case.

Error 'Bundle must tip at least 1000 lamports' appears when a bundle carries no tip or an undefined tip amount; one reported case logged 'Bundle tip: undefined SOL'. The fix is a SOL transfer of at least 1,000 lamports to a Jito tip account inside the bundle.

Block Engine auction rules per Jito's docs: parallel auctions run at 50 ms ticks; bundles whose account locks intersect (write-write, read-write, write-read) compete in one auction and others in separate auctions; ordering inside an auction is by requested tip per requested compute unit; Jito sends the highest-paying combination up to a compute-unit limit. A tight compute-unit limit therefore raises a bundle's tip efficiency, which RPC Fast also advises.

Hardcoded tips fail silently: a bundle with too small a tip is accepted but not selected, so logs show successful submissions while landing is poor (Troop's composite case used a fixed 0.0001 SOL tip; RPC Fast calls a static 100,000-lamport tip too high in quiet hours and too low in congestion). The live tip_floor distribution moved by an order of magnitude between 2024-09 and 2026-11 (median 10,000 to about 1,037 lamports; 95th about 1.45M to about 45k), so any constant tuned once goes stale. Read tip_floor or the tip_stream websocket and cap the bid by expected profit.

A Ledger signer moves the trust boundary onto the device. solana-keychain's SECURITY_MODEL.md says the private key never leaves the device, the PIN and on-device approval cannot be bypassed from the host, and the device handles one confirmation at a time, so a second signing request while a prompt is open is refused, not queued. The CLI selects a device with a `usb://` URL, and `Signer::is_interactive` exists so callers can tell that signing needs a person. Inference: a hardware wallet cannot serve an unattended or high-rate bot.

Total fee = base fee (5,000 lamports per signature, 50% burned) + priority fee (100% to the validator under SIMD-0096). The fee is deducted from the fee payer before execution and is still charged if the transaction fails, so an oversized limit or price is paid on failed attempts too.

Agave's scheduler ranks queued transactions by priority = reward x 1,000,000 / (1 + cost). Reward is the validator's fee income: the priority fee plus the non-burned share of the base fee. Cost is the cost-model total for signatures, write locks, instruction data, program execution (the requested or default CU limit) and loaded-accounts data. Rank therefore depends on lamports per unit of total requested cost, not on the micro-lamport price alone.

Standard bot pattern for compute sizing: simulate the transaction, read unitsConsumed, then set SetComputeUnitLimit to unitsConsumed times a margin. Chainstack uses ceil(unitsConsumed * 1.1) and says 10-20%; the Helius Rust SDK defaults to a 1.25 multiplier. The web3.js estimate utility warns real consumption 'might be higher or lower' than simulated, so a fixed margin is needed. Priority fee is charged on the requested limit, not actual use, so over-reserving costs money.

Neither common estimator has a fallback when the simulation returns no `unitsConsumed`. The web3.js estimator throws `SOLANA_ERROR__TRANSACTION__FAILED_TO_ESTIMATE_COMPUTE_LIMIT`, and the Helius Rust SDK returns `Error fetching compute units for the instructions provided`. The web3.js code also clamps the u64 value to u32 before it builds `SetComputeUnitLimit`.

To get a usable compute-unit number, simulate a test transaction that carries SetComputeUnitLimit of 1,400,000 (the per-transaction maximum). Without it the node applies the default of 200,000 units per non-compute-budget instruction, so a heavier transaction can fail the simulation before it reports its real usage. Helius pairs this test transaction with replaceRecentBlockhash: true and sigVerify: false.

The node that serves a simulation decides its result, so node lag or an RPC mismatch makes a valid transaction fail simulation. Three reports agree. Solana's retry guide: a blockhash from an advanced pool backend sent to a lagging backend is dropped. Helius, 'Mismatched RPCs': the node that checks validity can be behind the node that supplied the blockhash. program-metadata issue 105 (opened 2026-08-10): compute-unit estimation simulated each chunk write without minContextSlot on a hosted devnet RPC, failed with 'Invalid account data for instruction (instruction #3)', and left a rent-paid, par

The Rust Signer trait separates infallible and fallible calls, and the infallible ones hide failure. pubkey() and sign_message() default to try_pubkey() / try_sign_message() with unwrap_or_default(), returning the all-zeros Pubkey or Signature when the signer cannot act. A local Keypair never fails (its try_sign_message always returns Ok and is_interactive is false), but remote or hardware signers report SignerError variants such as Connection, NoDeviceFound and UserCancel, so bot code that signs through a remote signer should call the try_* methods and check is_interactive.

In the Rust `Signer` trait, the infallible `sign_message` returns an all-zeros `Signature` when signing is not possible; only `try_sign_message` returns a `SignerError`. That enum has variants for remote and hardware signers (`Connection`, `Protocol`, `NoDeviceFound`, `UserCancel`). The in-memory `Keypair` never fails (`try_sign_message` always returns Ok) and reports `is_interactive() == false`. Inference: a bot that switches from a `Keypair` to a remote or hardware signer and keeps calling `sign_message` can attach a zero signature without seeing an error. Call the `try_` form.

Error 'The supplied pubkey is not authorized to generate a token' (gRPC 7 PERMISSION_DENIED) means the client still passes an auth keypair to a Block Engine that no longer needs one for default sends. Jito says to pass Null or None for the auth key, and a gist commenter confirmed that removing the keypair from searcherClient(blockEngineUrl, authKeypair) fixed it.

DBI error and limit behaviour: HTTP 401 means no valid UUID in x-jito-auth; HTTP 429 means the per-key limit was exceeded (applied separately at each BAM node; QUIC drops excess packets instead; the numeric limit is set when the key is issued and not published); QUIC application close code 2 means the keypair is not allowlisted or not yet active, or connections from one IP arrive too fast, so reconnect with backoff, not in a tight loop.

SIMD-0096 (Activated) lists a known drawback of paying 100% of priority fees to the leader: a leader can inflate the priority fees reported in its own blocks at little cost, which 'could lead wallets to overestimate the required priority fee'. Estimators that read recent-block fees inherit this risk.

Addresses appended to a table are not usable in the slot they were added. The proposal says newly appended addresses need one slot to warm up, the program source says a table can only be used to look up addresses extended before the current bank's slot, and tutorials say to wait for the next slot after extend. A bot that extends and then immediately sends or simulates a transaction using the new entries will fail.

A deactivated table can still be used by transactions until its deactivation slot is no longer present in the SlotHashes sysvar. The table cannot be closed until then. The cool-down exists so in-flight transactions can land and to remove nondeterminism from loading addresses in the slot a table is closed.

The program source says it returns a generic error, not a specific one, for deactivated lookup tables, because a specific error would race with the table being closed at any point. A bot caching table accounts can therefore see a generic not-found style failure for a table that was deactivated, not a self-explanatory one.

Failing to pass the router's lookup tables when compiling the v0 message yields an oversized transaction. In solana-go issue 173 a Jupiter swap built without the tables came out at 1964 bytes against the 1232 limit. The reporter suspected the table wiring, and a later commenter (2025-12-21) said the fix was to fetch each addressLookupTableAddresses account, decode it, and pass the table map to the transaction builder with message version v0. The issue never confirms a root cause.

Lookup tables are a v0-only feature. A legacy message cannot reference a table, and a v0 message resolves a table only if the builder passes it in at compile time, for example compileToV0Message([lookupTableAccount]) in web3.js. The version lives in the first byte: when the high bit is set, the low 7 bits are the version number, so v0 starts with 0x80 and v1 with 0x81.

A deactivated table stays usable for lookups until its deactivation slot leaves the SlotHashes sysvar, which holds MAX_ENTRIES = 512 entries. While the slot is still present the table reports Deactivating with remaining_blocks = 512 minus the slot's position in SlotHashes (513 in the deactivation slot itself), and CloseLookupTable fails with 'Table cannot be closed until it's fully deactivated in {} blocks'. Close also fails on a table that is still active ('Lookup table is not deactivated'). The cool-down lets in-flight transactions land and stops a table from being closed and re-created for

A bad lookup fails as one of four TransactionError variants: AddressLookupTableNotFound ('Address lookup table not found'), InvalidAddressLookupTableOwner ('Attempted to lookup addresses from an account owned by the wrong program'), InvalidAddressLookupTableData ('Attempted to lookup addresses from an invalid account') or InvalidAddressLookupTableIndex ('Address table lookup uses an invalid index'). The SDK builds them from AddressLoaderError. Going over the lock limit gives TooManyAccountLocks ('Transaction locked too many accounts').

Once a table is fully deactivated, lookups return LookupTableAccountNotFound, the same error as for a missing table. The source explains why: a specific 'deactivated' error would race with the table being closed at any moment. The SDK maps it to TransactionError::AddressLookupTableNotFound. A bot that cached a table and now sees 'Address lookup table not found' should assume the authority deactivated the table, and should re-fetch the router's current table list.

CreateLookupTable takes a recent_slot that must appear in the SlotHashes sysvar. If it does not, the program logs '{slot} is not a recent slot' and fails with InvalidInstructionData. SlotHashes holds at most 512 entries, so slots older than that window are rejected. The table address is derived from the authority, the slot (little-endian) and a bump seed, so a table cannot be re-created at an address used before. The payer must sign.

When custom instructions push a Jupiter swap past 1,232 bytes there are three levers. (a) Lower maxAccounts in small steps: Jupiter now advises 'reducing 2 and retry', and warns that too low a value severely degrades routing (values under about 50 may give no route or a worse price); its older Metis example loops down from 64 by 1, with 1,244 bytes at 57 and 56 maxAccounts and 1,213 bytes at 51. (b) Drop createAssociatedTokenAccountIdempotent setup instructions for accounts that already exist, at the cost of one getAccountInfo call per account. (c) Request a v1 transaction for the 4,096-byte l

Building a router swap without the router's lookup tables produces an oversize transaction. In solana-go issue 173 (opened 2024-02-14, still open on 2026-11-06) the builder produced 1,964 bytes against the 1,232 limit, and four more users reported the same problem through 2025-05. A commenter on 2025-12-21 reported the fix: fetch every account in addressLookupTableAddresses, decode it, pass the table-to-addresses map to the transaction builder, and set the message version to v0. No maintainer confirmed the cause.

SIMD-0596 (status Draft on 2026-11-06, created 2026-08-11, by an Anza author) would raise the v1 account limit from 64 to 96 and keep legacy and v0 at 64. It states that the goal is to 'eventually remove support' for legacy and v0, so it deliberately does not raise their limits. It names no activation date or feature gate. Chainstack still calls v0 'not deprecated'. Do not plan around 96 accounts or a v0 sunset date yet.

blockSubscribe gives no JSON-RPC error when it meets a v1 transaction without the parameter: the notification carries block: null and an err of UnsupportedTransactionVersion. In Agave v4.3.0's rpc_subscriptions.rs the error branch emits {slot, block: None, err} and deliberately does not advance the last-notified slot, so the next trigger retries it. QuickNode says the subscription wedges on the first v1 slot; Chainstack says notifications keep arriving. Treat block: null as a failure, not an empty block, and alert on a stale subscription.

Table faults surface as generic transaction errors. An index past the active entries (for example right after an extend) returns InvalidLookupIndex, reported as 'Transaction address table lookup uses an invalid index'. A missing table, or one deactivated past its cool-down, returns 'Transaction loads an address table account that doesn't exist'. A wrong owner or bad data gives 'Transaction loads an address table account with an invalid owner' or '... with invalid data'. The code returns the generic not-found error for deactivated tables on purpose, because a specific error would race with the

CreateLookupTable takes a recent_slot that must appear in the SlotHashes sysvar. If it does not, the program logs '{slot} is not a recent slot' and fails with InvalidInstructionData. SlotHashes holds at most 512 entries, so the slot must be one of the last 512 produced. The table address is a PDA derived from the authority and that slot, and the program rejects any other address. Closed tables cannot be re-created at the same address. The program checks only that the payer signed.

FreezeLookupTable makes a table permanently immutable: it can never be extended or closed again, and its authority becomes none. Empty tables and deactivated tables cannot be frozen. A bot that depends on a third-party table can read the authority field. A frozen table can no longer gain entries or be closed out from under the bot.

Legacy and v0 stay valid after v1 activation and keep the 1,232-byte cap. Chainstack states v0 is not deprecated and lookup tables stay fully supported on it. The Solana upgrade guide calls moving from ALTs to v1 optional and says v0 keeps working. Sending v1 is opt-in. Reading v1 is not.

SIMD-0596 (Draft, created 2026-08-11) would raise the v1 account cap from 64 to 96 while legacy and v0 stay at 64. Solana's upgrade page lists it as in development, tentatively after Agave 4.5, with no feature gate and no Agave release containing it. Until it activates, v1 transactions above 64 accounts are rejected. The SIMD also says the increase_tx_account_lock_limit feature, a 128-account limit, must be removed first.

A bot can cache a table's contents and re-fetch only to pick up new entries or to notice deactivation, meaning a deactivation_slot other than the maximum value in the table meta. Append-only entries and no re-creation at the same address mean a cached index never changes meaning. A cached copy that lacks a new entry cannot reference it, and a closed table makes the transaction fail.

Deduplicate the account list before building a message. TransactionError AccountLoadedTwice ('Account loaded twice') rejects a message whose account_keys repeat a key, although instructions may reference one key many times, and the Anza proposal bars loading an account both directly and through a table. DFlow and QuickNode describe duplicates as tolerated before v1, which the error enum contradicts.

Blockhash and signature rules for simulateTransaction. With the defaults (replaceRecentBlockhash false, sigVerify false) the transaction needs a recent blockhash the node still accepts, but it does not need valid signatures. replaceRecentBlockhash: true makes the node swap in its bank's latest blockhash and report it as replacementBlockhash. sigVerify: true checks signatures. The two flags conflict: sending both returns an invalid-params error, 'sigVerify may not be used with replaceRecentBlockhash'.

Transactions are submitted to the Block Engine (JSON-RPC POST /api/v1/bundles, method sendBundle, or gRPC) as base64 strings (recommended); base58 is slow and marked DEPRECATED in Jito's docs. Maximum 5 transactions per request.

sendBundle (JSON-RPC, path /api/v1/bundles) returns a bundle ID, the SHA-256 hash of the bundle's transaction signatures, once the Block Engine has received the bundle. That is an acceptance receipt, not a landing guarantee. A tip that is too low does not fail the call; the bundle may simply not be selected in the auction. Confirm landing with getBundleStatuses or getInflightBundleStatuses, or by checking the transaction signatures on chain.

Open reference code: jito-labs/bam-dbi holds Rust clients for DBI JSON-RPC and QUIC with legacy, v0 and v1 transfer examples; the community jito-bundle crate adds a random tip account, tip-floor fetching (FetchFloor and FetchFloorWithCap strategies), per-transaction and Helius simulateBundle simulation, fail-over across five Block Engine endpoints, polling that handles 429s and timeouts, and typed errors such as TooManyTransactions, SimulationFailed and ConfirmationTimeout.

Standard method for sizing the limit: simulate the transaction with a high placeholder limit, read unitsConsumed, then set SetComputeUnitLimit to that value plus a 10-20% margin. The margin covers state changes between simulation and execution; the simulated figure can be higher or lower than what the landed transaction uses.

Set SetComputeUnitLimit from a simulation. Simulate with a high placeholder limit, read unitsConsumed, then add a margin. The sources use 5% to 20%: Chainstack 10% (10-20% in its workflow), OrbitFlare 10-20%, a swap-routing team 12% (10-15%), QuickNode examples 5% and 10%. The margin covers state changes between simulation and landing.

An inflated CU limit costs fees and scheduling priority. The cost model counts the requested CU limit (and a cost for requested loaded-account data) against block and per-account limits, and releases the unused part only after execution (SIMD-0170 motivation). Scheduler priority is reward divided by total cost (Anza), so extra requested units lower it. Example: a swap that uses 75,000 CUs but requests 1,400,000 CUs at 50,000 micro-lamports/CU pays 70,000 lamports.

Because requested CUs sit in the cost denominator, a tighter CU limit (and a tighter loaded-accounts data limit) raises a transaction's rank at the same total lamport fee, while raising only the price spends more for the same cost. A practitioner post argues that right-sizing the CU limit moves rank more than a higher price does.

The fee cache skips simple vote transactions, transactions with invalid compute budget data or account locks, and transactions whose compute unit limit is 0. The RPC value stays in micro-lamports per CU for v1 traffic: Agave derives the price as floor(priority_fee_lamports x 1,000,000 / compute_unit_limit). A legacy or v0 transaction whose fee was rounded up can therefore show a price slightly above the one it requested.

To size the limit, build the transaction with SetComputeUnitLimit at 1,400,000, simulate it, read unitsConsumed, then set the limit to unitsConsumed times a margin. Advice on the margin varies: Solana's docs say 10%, Chainstack 10-20%, a swap-routing team 10-15% (12% in its code), QuickNode's web3.js samples use 5% and its Kit samples 10%, and Jupiter says at least 1.2x.

Leaving the default or 1.4M limit costs money and block space. A swap that uses 75,000 CUs but requests 1,400,000 at 50,000 micro-lamports per CU pays 70,000 lamports, against 3,750 lamports at a 75,000 limit (4,200 with a 12% margin). SIMD-0170 adds that the runtime holds over-allocated CUs in the block cost tracker until execution finishes and releases them afterwards, which lowers block density and can push a request past a hot account's remaining per-block allowance.

Skipping preflight also skips the node-health check, so a node that is behind still accepts and forwards the transaction. Solana's retry guide says preflight can detect a lagging RPC pool at submission, calls preflight 'often the difference between losing a transaction and allowing a client to gracefully handle an error', and recommends keeping `skipPreflight` false. The guide text is the archived January 2025 version; the live page was not readable.

A transaction that lands and fails still pays its fee, so every failure that `skipPreflight` lets onto the chain costs money that a failing preflight would have saved. Solana's fee docs say the fee is still collected for failed transactions, and Agave's simulation code has a `FeesOnly` outcome for transactions that fail to load but still pay a fee.

Aggregators can run the simulation for you. Jupiter's v6 /swap parameter dynamicComputeUnitLimit does a swap simulation to set the compute-unit limit and, per its own spec, 'will increase latency slightly since there will be one extra RPC call to simulate this'. QuickNode's Jupiter guide says the API returns a simulated transaction, so skipPreflight can be set true. Jupiter's current docs page says the Metis Swap API is superseded by Swap V2, so these parameter docs may be stale.

Generic HTTP retry is not enough for transaction sends. Retrying the same request after a BlockhashNotFound or expiry error fails, so the handler must fetch a fresh blockhash, re-sign and resend. Aggressive retry adds network load and each rebuilt attempt can cost fees; fail fast and alert when the RPC is badly degraded.

Agave simulates with a maximum blockhash age of `max_processing_age` minus `MAX_TRANSACTION_FORWARDING_DELAY`, and a code comment says this stops a transaction expiring while it is forwarded to the leader. With the solana-sdk constants (150 and 6) the limit is 144 slots, so a simulation can report `BlockhashNotFound` for a blockhash the leader would still accept.

A 'Blockhash not found' error can come from a commitment mismatch. If the blockhash is fetched at confirmed but the RPC checks validity at finalized (the preflightCommitment default), the checker's view lags the transaction's blockhash. Fix: fetch the blockhash at confirmed and set preflightCommitment to the same level, even when skipPreflight is true.

'Blockhash not found' has four separate causes. (a) The blockhash expired. (b) The bank used by preflight or simulation is older than the blockhash, from a commitment mismatch or a lagging RPC. (c) The blockhash came from a minority fork at processed. (d) Signing was slow: a code-payments Android PR merged 2026-05-20 found that a Phantom round trip over about 60 s expired the blockhash, and the app wrongly told users to check their USDC and SOL balance. With about 32 s of lifetime now, the signing budget is about half of that figure.

The simulateTransaction config has seven fields in solana-rpc-client-api 4.4.1: `sigVerify`, `replaceRecentBlockhash`, `commitment`, `encoding`, `accounts`, `minContextSlot` and `innerInstructions`. The three booleans default to false. If `encoding` is omitted, Agave decodes the payload as base58, so a bot that sends base64 must set `encoding: 'base64'`; Solana's docs call base58 slow and deprecated.

For compute estimation Helius calls `simulateTransaction` with `replaceRecentBlockhash: true` and `sigVerify: false`, so the transaction needs no signature and cannot fail on blockhash age. Helius's 2024 blockhash guide gives the same advice for any simulateTransaction call, and the Agave source shows that the two flags are valid together in this combination.

Triton, Chainstack and OrbitFlare tell latency-sensitive senders to call `simulateTransaction` as its own request and then send with `skipPreflight: true`. Triton says its preflight is a separate blocking step that fails the send if the simulation cannot run; Chainstack names arbitrage and sniping; OrbitFlare says traders often skip simulation to save milliseconds. These vendors sell RPC or landing services, and none publishes a latency measurement.

Infrastructure vendors tell latency-sensitive senders to run simulateTransaction as a separate call and send with skipPreflight: true. Triton says that with skipPreflight false it runs the preflight simulation as a separate, blocking step before it forwards the send, and fails the send if that simulation cannot run. Chainstack names arbitrage and sniping as the use case for skipPreflight. OrbitFlare says traders often skip simulation to save milliseconds. None of the three publishes a measurement of the time saved, and all three sell RPC or landing services.

Always pass encoding base64 to simulateTransaction and sendTransaction. The docs call base58 slow, the default base58 form is capped at 1,232 bytes, and a v1 transaction larger than that must be sent as base64 (Chainstack: base64 accepts up to 4,096 raw bytes). A request with the default encoding and a larger transaction fails with a 'too large' error.

A timeout says nothing about the transaction's fate. web3.js 1.x fails with 'Transaction was not confirmed in 30.00 seconds. It is unknown if it succeeded or failed.' The fardream library notes that the older sendAndConfirmTransaction flow just waits 60 s and cannot tell a dropped transaction from a slow one. A Drift keeper log shows the same message next to 'This transaction has already been processed', and a Drift maintainer attributes it to congestion or an RPC node that falls behind. Look up the signature and compare block height with lastValidBlockHeight before retrying.

Open report: web3.js issue 35556 (solana-labs/solana, 2024-05-14) says connection.confirmTransaction at confirmed threw the block-height-exceeded error for a transaction that had already finalized. A bot closed it by pointing to the Agave repo and no root cause was given. LI.FI's findings (polling a borrowed block height, no final status lookup) are plausible mechanisms, but nobody confirmed them for this issue. Check the signature status before treating an expiry exception as proof of failure.

Jito-Solana RPC supports simulateBundle to check a whole bundle before submission, and Helius exposes it with an encodedTransactions parameter under its general RPC rate limit. Jito's advice for a bundle that is not landing starts with validating the transactions and the bundle by simulation.

Static tips fail under congestion. Gerus Lab reports that a hard-coded 0.005 SOL tip stopped landing during congestion, and RPC Fast calls a static 100,000-lamport tip too high in quiet hours and too low in congestion. Both recommend telemetry-driven dynamic tips with a profit-based cap. RPC Fast puts the competitive ceiling at 50-70% of expected profit; that is a vendor estimate with no published data.

Alternatives to Jito submission trade away atomicity or coverage. Gerus Lab (a vendor blog) says QuickNode's Lil-JIT cannot guarantee atomic multi-transaction execution, and that Astralane's private relay has smaller validator coverage than Jito and an extra relay hop. RPC Fast says some of Jito's tip share moved to Astralane and Lil-JIT in Q1 2026. Neither source publishes measurements.

Rate limits: Jito's docs give the Block Engine default as 1 request per second per IP per region, with no auth key needed for default sends; over the limit you get a 429 or rate-limit error, and higher limits go through a Discord ticket. The default was 5 requests/s until commit fa0e59a on 2025-02-22, so sources still quoting 5 req/s predate that change. Helius limits its sendBundle proxy to 5 requests/s per project (a different layer); DBI limits are per key per BAM node and unpublished.

Key material in telemetry is a theft route. In August 2022 security firm Otter reported that Slope's mobile wallet sent users' seed phrases over TLS to a centralized Sentry server where they sat as readable text. Sentry said 9,231 Solana wallets were drained from 22:37 UTC on 2 August 2022 over four hours, that the keys went to a host (o7e[.]slope[.]finance) it believes was a self-hosted Sentry, that its SaaS was not implicated, and that it added scrubbing so 'privatekey' and 'private_key' fields are not stored. Keep key bytes out of logs and error reporters.

Agave master (commit 92a5cd130, checked 2026-11-06) has two block-production methods: central-scheduler (deprecated, with a warning to use the greedy one) and central-scheduler-greedy (the default). The greedy scheduler 'will attempt to schedule in priority order, scheduling anything that can be immediately scheduled, up to the limits'. Priority order is therefore best effort: a lower-priority transaction with no lock conflict can run while a conflicting higher-priority one waits. Lehran Brothers (February 2024) and Helius (June 2024) describe a multi-iterator scheduler with independent per-th

Two parts of the scheduler cost do not depend on the CU limit: 720 CUs per signature (30 x 24) and 300 CUs per writable account (30 x 10). Instruction-data cost, loaded-accounts-data cost and the program execution cost (the CU limit) are added on top.

The result carries err, logs (null if simulation failed before execution, e.g. invalid blockhash or signature failure), unitsConsumed (u64), returnData (most recent, with programId and base64 data) and an optional accounts array matching the request's accounts.addresses. If err is non-null the accounts entries are null.

To size `SetComputeUnitLimit`, simulate a copy of the transaction with a high placeholder limit, read `unitsConsumed`, then rebuild with that value plus a margin. Helius's optimizing-transactions page, its manual-send guide and its Rust SDK all use 1_400_000 as the placeholder so the simulation itself cannot run out of compute. The web3.js estimator PR used u32::MAX instead, and its author measured the same count as a value below 1.4M because the runtime clamps the limit.

Wallet simulation can also be wrong in the other direction. Phantom 26.11.0 showed 'This transaction reverted during simulation. Funds may be lost if submitted.' on every devnet transaction from one dapp, although the transaction succeeded when signed; Solflare and Backpack showed no warning. The issue (phantom/docs #489, opened 2026-04-13) was still open, with no Phantom reply on the page, on 2026-11-06.

A wallet's own simulation can disagree with the cluster. Phantom docs issue 489 (opened 2026-04-13; Phantom 26.11.0, Chrome 146, devnet) reports that every transaction from one dapp triggered 'This transaction reverted during simulation. Funds may be lost if submitted.', yet signing anyway landed and executed successfully. Solflare and Backpack showed no warning for the same transactions. This is one unresolved user report.

A 32-byte seed is not a 64-byte keypair, and the constructors treat them differently. Rust keypair_from_seed returns 'Seed is too short' under 32 bytes and otherwise uses only seed[..32], so longer input (for example a 64-byte BIP-39 seed) is accepted and truncated without error. web3.js Keypair.fromSeed has no length check of its own and builds secretKey as the seed followed by the derived public key. In solders, from_seed takes a 32-byte seed, from_bytes takes the 64-byte keypair, and the mnemonic example passes seed[:32].

Limit the blast radius of a file wallet. Metaplex's matrix pairs local testing with a no-passphrase file wallet, devnet/testnet with a file wallet and backed-up seed, small mainnet amounts with a passphrase-protected file wallet on an encrypted disk, and significant value with a hardware wallet or multisig; it also says never to reuse a keypair across mainnet testing and production. Anza likewise says large balances should not sit in a file system wallet. For a bot, that points to a dedicated hot key funded only with working capital (inference).

Once a blockhash has expired, resending the same signed bytes cannot succeed: the handler must fetch a fresh blockhash, re-sign and resend, and a generic HTTP retry wrapper does not do that. Retries consume blockhashes and can cost fees, and no retry strategy rescues a badly degraded network, so fail fast and alert.

A fixed client timeout cannot tell a dropped transaction from a slow one. Web3.js sendAndConfirmTransaction waits 60 seconds and then throws with no way to tell whether the transaction was dropped, and Drift's SDK threw 'It is unknown if it succeeded or failed' after 30 seconds. Use lastValidBlockHeight as the expiry signal and keep timeouts as a backstop.

If the retry pool is full, or the request set maxRetries to 0, the node broadcasts the transaction once and never retries it. The Solana retry guide says overflow transactions are 'dropped'. The code shows the first broadcast has already happened: send_transactions_in_batch runs first, then 'if retry_len >= retry_pool_max_size { break; }' skips the insert, and 'if max_retries == Some(0) { continue; }' skips it too. The Config comment reads 'new transactions are dropped after their first broadcast attempt'. A bot cannot count on node-side rebroadcast when it sets maxRetries 0 or when the node's

Bundles execute only when a Jito-Solana leader is producing the block; standard validator clients never receive them. If no Jito leader is upcoming, the Block Engine drops the bundle (error text seen in the wild: 'Bundle Dropped, no connected leader up soon'; proto DroppedBundle comment: 'e.g. because no leader upcoming'). A community pattern polls the next scheduled leader and sends only when it is within about 2 slots.

Jito's default send rate limit is 1 request per second per IP per region, with no auth key needed for default sends; exceeding it returns a 429 or rate-limit error; higher limits need a ticket. Spreading sends across regional Block Engine endpoints (mainnet global plus Amsterdam, Dublin, Frankfurt and others) therefore multiplies capacity.
Jito's documented default limit is 1 request per second per IP per region; a higher limit needs a support ticket. This number comes from one source, Jito's docs, and no second source confirms it.

Wrapping a sandwich-prone transaction in your own bundle keeps an attacker from including it in a sandwich bundle, because bundles cannot be nested on Jito. Jupiter's MEV-protection setting works this way by issuing a length-one bundle. The IMC authors caution that this does not stop all front-running, and Solana's guide adds that tight slippage is the most effective single defense.

Do not compare vendor landing rates without a stated denominator. RPC Fast's own Q1 2026 benchmark (about 50,000 paired submissions, labelled illustrative) lists 94% bundle landing on its dedicated tier against under 30% on public RPC. Jito's own BAM funnel shows an end-to-end land rate of 0.57% of received bundles for 20 Sep-7 Oct 2026 (0.45% for 3-20 Sep), because most received bundles fail simulation (simulation success 16.1%).

Jito's docs, restructured on 2026-11-05, describe two bundle paths. Block Engine: public, reaches BAM and non-BAM Jito leaders, default limit 1 request/s per IP per region. Direct Bundle Ingest (DBI): goes straight to a BAM Node over JSON-RPC or QUIC, serves BAM leaders only, is allowlisted, and uses credentials separate from the Block Engine (a Block Engine UUID or gRPC key does not grant DBI access).

BAM, the leader set that DBI serves, held 164M SOL across 385 validators, 37% of total stake, at epoch 1050 (BAM changelog, 2026-10-09). SolanaFloor figures quoted by Solana Compass give 34.1% (383 of 665 active validators) on 2026-09-09 and about 12% in January 2026. A DBI-only sender therefore cannot land in the slots of the remaining ~63% of stake; the Block Engine path covers BAM and non-BAM Jito leaders.

Multi-endpoint submission with fail-over: FullSend's regional direct endpoints (ewr1, fra1, tyo1; your server IPs must be allowlisted) recommend a 1,000 ms timeout and moving to the next-nearest region on timeout or error; the jito-bundle crate tries the next of five Block Engine endpoints on failure; RPC Fast advises parallel multi-region submission. The Block Engine's default limit is worded per IP per region, so each regional endpoint has its own 1 request/s budget by the docs' wording.

Transport-security caveats in Jito's own docs: the FullSend regional direct endpoints use self-signed TLS and the docs' Rust example sets danger_accept_invalid_certs(true); the DBI JSON-RPC endpoint is documented as plain http on port 9090 with the UUID in a request header. In both cases a client cannot authenticate the server or hide the signed transaction (and, on DBI JSON-RPC, the credential) from the network path.

Leaving the default CU limit hurts twice: the fee is computed on the inflated request, and the scheduler ranks by price per CU while filling blocks by requested compute, so a transaction requesting 200,000 CUs but using about 500 takes block space from others. Block caps cited: 48,000,000 CUs per block and 12,000,000 CUs per account per block.

SetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit: with no explicit limit, a transaction is charged for loading up to 64 MB of account data at 8 CU per 32 KB (about 16,000 CU). Anza argues requesting only the bytes needed lowers the CU total and so raises priority (reward divided by CU) without changing the fee; its worked token-transfer example moves the score from 0.30 to 0.63.

Current Agave clamps a CU limit above 1,400,000 to 1,400,000. It does not reject the transaction: sanitize_and_convert_to_compute_budget_limits applies .min(MAX_COMPUTE_UNIT_LIMIT). A 2024 feature-gate proposal to fail such transactions (solana-labs/solana issue 35517) was closed by a bot the day it was filed, with a pointer to re-open it in anza-xyz/agave, and master (commit 92a5cd130) still clamps.

Without SetLoadedAccountsDataSizeLimit a transaction may load up to 64 MiB of account data. The cost model charges 8 CUs per 32 KiB page of the requested limit, so the default adds 16,384 CUs to the transaction's cost. Anza's worked token-transfer example (Nov 2024) shows the priority score rising from 0.30 to 0.63 when the limit drops from 64 MB to 10 MB. Request only the data the transaction needs; a value of 0 is invalid.

Code that reads limits or fees by scanning Compute Budget instructions finds nothing on v1 transactions. Read transactionConfig first and fall back to the instruction scan for legacy and v0. To compare a v0 rate with a v1 total, convert the rate with ceil(price * CU limit / 1,000,000). JSON-RPC readers need maxSupportedTransactionVersion set to the integer 1, or getBlock and getTransaction fail with error -32015 on v1 data.

The mainnet block limit is 100M CUs since epoch 1009 (2026-07-29) under SIMD-0286 (status Activated), up from 60M (SIMD-0256, July 2025) and 50M before. Agave master defines both MAX_BLOCK_UNITS_SIMD_0256 (60M) and MAX_BLOCK_UNITS_SIMD_0286 (100M). Solana Compass reports that SIMD-0525 scales per-slot limits in proportion to slot time, so the room per 200 ms block is smaller than the headline figure; the exact per-slot cap was not verified.

Averages, medians or percentiles of the raw per-slot values are statistics of floors, not of what landed transactions paid. In congestion the distribution above the floor widens where this call cannot see it, so such estimates run low exactly when it matters. The reverse also happens: one overpaying transaction on a quiet account sets that account's value for the whole slot. Triton calls the default value often zero and a poor signal for the competitive fee.

If the limit is below the CUs the transaction needs, execution stops with InstructionError::ComputationalBudgetExceeded ('Computational budget exceeded') and the fee is still charged. Simulation can understate later usage because state moves between simulation and landing (routes, tick arrays, Token-2022 transfer hooks). A variable-cost swap therefore needs a larger margin than a fixed-cost transfer, and a re-simulation close to submission.

Current per-block limits depend on slot time. SIMD-0286 raised the block limit from 60M to 100M CUs at epoch 1009 (2026-07-29), and SIMD-0306 sets the writable-account limit to 40% of the block limit. SIMD-0525 scales per-slot limits with slot time, so at the 200 ms slots live since epoch 1053 (2026-10-09) the limits are 50M CUs per block and 20M CUs per writable account (vote 18M). Chainstack and a 2026 swap-routing blog still quote 48M/12M, and Solana's compute-budget page (pinned to Agave v3.1.8) lists 60M/12M and calls SIMD-0286 a proposal; QuickNode's 2026-10-21 figures of 50M/20M match t

A request may not list more addresses than the transaction has account keys (Agave error `Too many accounts provided; max N`), base58 is not supported as the account encoding, and every entry is null when the transaction errors.

kora-lib 2.0.5 loader quirks not to copy: the file-path check runs before the format checks, so any string naming a readable file is parsed as a keypair file; the JSON error text promises an object with a 'keypair' field that the parser does not accept; the crate adds no public-key consistency check of its own and relies on `Keypair::try_from`; and its tests include no wrong-length base58 case. A loader written for a bot should test those cases itself.

The docs say `logs` is null when simulation fails before execution. Agave v4.4.1 returns `logs: []` and `unitsConsumed: 0` for a `BlockhashNotFound` simulation, and its tests assert that shape. A bot should test `err` first and must not use `logs === null` as the failure signal.

A Jito bundle is a list of up to 5 fully signed transactions that execute sequentially, within a single slot, and atomically: if any transaction fails, none are committed. Bundles cannot cross slot boundaries.

A Jito bundle is a list of up to 5 fully signed transactions that the Block Engine passes to a Jito-Solana leader to execute sequentially and atomically within one slot. A bundle cannot cross a slot boundary, and if any transaction fails none of the transactions are committed.

When a Block Engine rate limit is exceeded the response is HTTP 429 or a rate-limit error that names the limit hit, and Jito says default sends no longer need an approved auth key. The jito-bundle Rust crate treats 429s, timeouts and on-chain failures as separate cases in its status handling.

Two failover patterns exist. RPC Fast recommends sending the same bundle in parallel to several Block Engine regions (plus alternative relays and raw RPC as a fallback), letting the fastest arrival win, with leader-aware region weighting. The jito-bundle crate and Jito's FullSend docs instead fail over in sequence: the crate tries the next of its 5 endpoints on failure, and FullSend recommends a 1,000 ms timeout and then the next-closest region. Jito states its default limit per IP per region, which is the limit each leg of a fan-out runs against.

A Jito bundle is up to five fully signed transactions that run in the listed order, atomically and all-or-nothing, inside one slot (a bundle cannot cross a slot boundary). Only a leader running Jito-Solana or BAM can process it; Jito's docs say tips do nothing on leaders that are not Jito-Solana.
Resending identical signed bytes is harmless because the network executes at most one copy of a given signature. The duplicate risk comes only from building a second, different transaction.

A timeout is not a failure. Drift's SDK throws 'Transaction was not confirmed in 30 seconds. It is unknown if it succeeded or failed. Check signature ...', and a later simulation of a re-sent transaction reported 'This transaction has already been processed'. This is the symptom of a landed transaction the sender stopped tracking.

In the Rust EncodableKey::write_to_file path (solana-signer), the writer creates missing parent directories, opens the file with create + truncate (overwriting an existing file without warning) and sets mode 0o600 on Unix only; on non-Unix targets no mode is set. Because the mode applies at creation, an existing file likely keeps its old permissions (inferred, not stated in source). solana-keypair has a unix-only test asserting 0o600 after write_keypair_file.

Setting `sigVerify: true` together with `replaceRecentBlockhash: true` returns the JSON-RPC invalid-params error (-32602) with the message `sigVerify may not be used with replaceRecentBlockhash`. Agave's own unit test asserts this response, and Infura and Triton both document the two flags as conflicting.

A simulation that depends on a just-confirmed transaction can fail on a lagging RPC node with `Transaction simulation failed` and `Invalid account data for instruction (instruction #3)`, because that node has not seen the prerequisite yet. The program-metadata CU estimator hit this on a hosted devnet RPC because it simulated each chunk write without `minContextSlot`. The reporter suggests passing the confirmation slot as `minContextSlot` and retrying; a node below that slot answers error -32016 `Minimum context slot has not been reached`.

Agave's simulate path builds its batch with prepare_unlocked_batch_from_single_tx ('without locking accounts') and never commits the result. A passing simulation therefore says nothing about write-lock contention with other transactions or about scheduler and block-limit behavior. That consequence is an inference from the code; no doc states it.

Bots fail far more often than people on Solana. In the ISSTA 2025 study of landed failures, bot accounts failed 58.43% of their transactions (about 453.5 million failed against 322.6 million successful) and human accounts failed 6.22%, per arXiv v1. The ISSTA program abstract gives the bot figure as 73.4%. The numbers differ between versions of the same paper, so rely on the direction, not the figure.
Metaplex advises separate keypairs per purpose ('Never use the same keypair for mainnet testing and production') so test scripts cannot send real SOL.

The Solana CLI resolves a keypair argument from a file path, prompt: (seed-phrase prompt), usb://... (Ledger), stdin:, or the legacy ASK keyword (flagged in code as a legacy derivation to avoid in favour of prompt:); unknown URI schemes error. A bad file fails with 'could not read keypair file' plus a hint to run solana-keygen new. `solana-keygen pubkey <file>` prints the address, and `solana-keygen verify <PUBKEY> <file>` signs a test message and reports 'Success' or fails with 'Failed'. `new` takes --outfile, --force, --silent and --no-outfile; Metaplex documents --no-bip39-passphrase for sc

A simulation reflects one RPC node's view. If the node lags, a dependent simulation can fail with missing-account errors because it has not seen a just-confirmed transaction. The program-metadata CU estimator hit this on a hosted devnet RPC, and the suggested fix is to pass the confirmation slot as minContextSlot to simulateTransaction and to retry such simulations.

Moving web3.js v1 to v3 is a code change even though the class names survive. Keypair.generate/fromSecretKey/fromSeed, Transaction.sign/partialSign/serialize/verifySignatures and VersionedTransaction.sign become async (VersionedTransaction.serialize stays sync); serialize returns Uint8Array; legacy { publicKey, secretKey } signer objects are rejected, so pass a Keypair or another Kit signer; most RPC numerics (lamports, slots, block heights) are bigint; account data is Uint8Array and many RPC arrays are readonly; PublicKey.unique(), the Account class, the sync PDA helpers and the FeeCalculator

As of 2026-11-06 solana-py's latest tag is v0.41.0 (2026-10-03) while master has 19 later commits. A bot that installs from PyPI does not get these; one that installs from git master does.

solana-py does not accept a solders legacy Transaction in send_transaction: passing one raises AttributeError: 'solders.transaction.Transaction' object has no attribute 'recent_blockhash'. The maintainer called this unsupported rather than a bug, said a fix was due in 0.35.0, and a commenter still reported it on 0.35.1; the thread discusses removing solana-py's own Transaction class (PR #442).

Upgrading to web3.js v3 silently changes Connection's default commitment from finalized to confirmed. The code compiles unchanged, so the compiler cannot flag it; the official migration guide says 'omitted commitment now defaults to confirmed rather than finalized'. A bot that relied on finalized reads must pass the commitment explicitly on the Connection or per call, and should test against a real node because mocked tests keep passing with the old default.

Library floors for v1: web3.js 1.99.0 can read v1 but cannot build, sign or send it. Sending needs @solana/kit 8.0, web3.js 3.x, Agave 4.2-era Rust crates, solders 0.29.0 or solana-go 1.23.0. Chainstack lists kit 7.1.0 as the first release that reports version as the number 1 rather than 1n.

Triton reported that moving its Ping Thing service from web3.js to Kit cut average confirmation latency by about 200 ms with the same RPC config and unchanged slot latency. This is a vendor-run measurement with no published sample size, window or method, and it measures confirmation, not local signing. I found no independent benchmark of web3.js vs Kit signing cost.

The only SDK-versus-SDK performance numbers I found are vendor-run and narrow. Triton reports about 200 ms lower average confirmation latency in its Ping Thing after moving to Kit, with the same RPC config and unchanged slot latency, and publishes no sample size or window. I found no Node.js benchmark and no independent comparison.

Standard compute-unit sizing: simulate, read unitsConsumed, then set SetComputeUnitLimit to that value plus a margin. Solana's docs say add 10%. Chainstack says +10% (range 10-20%). Helius uses Math.ceil(unitsConsumed * 1.1). The Helius Rust SDK defaults to a 1.25 multiplier with a floor of 1000 units, citing simulation-versus-execution differences and worst-case paths. The web3.js estimator PR warns that real consumption 'might be higher or lower' than the simulation. Size tightly because the priority fee is charged on the requested limit, not on units used.

Alpenglow went live on mainnet-beta at slot 459,653,000 on 2026-10-21, and slot time reached 200 ms on 2026-10-09. Triton's simulateTransaction page and OrbitFlare's explainer both say `confirmed` and `finalized` now converge to the same state, with `finalized` arriving about 150 ms after a block instead of 32 slots later. This narrows Helius's 2024 warning about a `confirmed` blockhash being newer than a `finalized` preflight check. Solana bot tooling mostly takes keys from environment variables. Kora's `signers.example.toml` gives a memory signer a `private_key_env` field and shows `export SIGNER_1_PRIVATE_KEY` with a base58 value; every other Kora signer type, including Turnkey, Privy and Vault, also reads its credentials from environment variables named in the config. sol-trade-sdk's `load_keypair_from_env` and the Railway forum answer do the same. Inference: moving to a remote signer moves the secret (an API key or Vault token) into the environment rather than removing it.

Transaction V1 (SIMD-0385, with the size limit from SIMD-0296) activated on Solana mainnet at the first slot of epoch 1035 (slot 447,120,000) on 2026-09-15, via feature gate txv1aq4pp281K9um3tnPgkfX8UqtFT6wcVW3hNezGLL. Reports of the exact UTC time differ (about 01:04 vs 01:20).

Size cost of a v0 lookup, from the Anza proposal: 1 byte for the version, 1 byte for the lookup count, 34 bytes per table used (32-byte table key plus one length byte each for the writable and read-only index lists), and 1 byte per loaded account instead of 32. By that arithmetic a table that supplies only one account costs 35 bytes against 32 inline and loses; a table pays off from two accounts (36 bytes against 64). QuickNode reports the same effect: transactions that pull a few addresses from several tables get smaller when converted to v1.

The table authority must sign every extend, freeze, deactivate and close. Entries are append-only, so an index always resolves to the same address (Anza made tables append-only to stop front-running). FreezeLookupTable sets the authority to None; after that the program refuses extend, deactivate and close ('Lookup table is frozen'), so the table's rent is locked for good. A bot that depends on someone else's table, such as a router's, must expect the authority to deactivate and close it, and should re-fetch table accounts before building instead of caching them indefinitely.

Transaction V1 went live on Solana mainnet at the first slot of epoch 1035 (slot 447,120,000) on 2026-09-15, behind feature gate txv1aq4pp281K9um3tnPgkfX8UqtFT6wcVW3hNezGLL. The SIMD repository marks SIMD-0385 'Activated' (status change of 2026-10-28, checked against the feature accounts on 2026-10-26). Outlets disagree on the minute: about 01:04 UTC (Solana Compass) versus about 01:20 UTC (Crypto Briefing).

Each lookup table a v0 message references adds about 34 bytes: the 32-byte table address plus two length bytes. Each account loaded through a table then costs 1 byte instead of 32. By that arithmetic, one account from a table costs 3 bytes more than inlining it, and two or more save bytes. Solana Foundation figures: 40 accounts from one table cost about 74 lookup bytes, and the same 40 across ten tables cost about 380.

Most 'bad size' or 'not base58' load errors come from mixing two encodings of the same 64 bytes: the CLI keypair file is a JSON array of 64 numbers, while a Phantom 'Export Private Key' value is the base58 string of the same 64-byte keypair (Mazur notes it is the keypair, not just the private key). Load the array with solders Keypair.from_bytes or web3.js Keypair.fromSecretKey(new Uint8Array(JSON.parse(text))), and the string with Keypair.from_base58_string or bs58.decode.
